modules.title: Replicated jar tests and treatment constraints
objectives: Compare candidate doses within stated constraints.
Separate repeatability from a causal treatment conclusion.
modules.lesson:
### What a replicated jar test can and cannot prove

A jar test is a small, tightly controlled bench comparison run on one grab sample of raw water under one set of mixing and settling conditions. It produces a ranking of candidate doses for that water, on that day, measured on that turbidimeter, by that operator. It does not produce an authorized full-scale dose, and on its own it does not establish that the dose caused the difference you observed.

Two separate questions get confused constantly. The first is repeatability: if I run the same dose three times in the same session, how much do the answers scatter? The second is causation: is the gap between Dose A and Dose B larger than that scatter, and does it persist when the raw water, temperature and operator change? Replication answers the first question directly. It only contributes to the second question when the replicates are true replicates, meaning independently dosed jars rather than three readings from one jar or three readings of one cuvette.

Three readings of the same cuvette measure instrument noise. Three readings of three aliquots from one jar measure instrument noise plus sampling noise. Three independently dosed and independently settled jars measure instrument noise plus sampling noise plus dosing and mixing variability. Only the third one tells you whether the bench method can actually distinguish two doses. Label which kind of replication you ran on the bench sheet, because a reviewer cannot tell afterward and the three kinds give very different spreads.

Also be honest about what the response variable is. Settled supernatant turbidity is a proxy for floc formation and settleability. It is not filtered water turbidity, it is not filter run length, it is not residual aluminium, and it is not disinfection performance. A dose that wins on settled turbidity can lose on every one of those.

### Controlling everything except the dose

If anything other than dose varies systematically across jars, the apparent dose effect is confounded and the run is not interpretable. Fix and record the following for the whole run: raw water sample identity, time and location of collection, sample temperature at the time of dosing, raw turbidity, raw pH, raw alkalinity, coagulant product and lot, stock solution strength and preparation date, order and timing of chemical addition, rapid mix speed and duration, flocculation speed and duration, settling time, sampling depth for the supernatant, and the turbidimeter identifier with its last calibration and verification.

Temperature deserves particular attention. Cold water slows flocculation kinetics and raises viscosity, so a fixed settling time penalises a dose more at 3 degrees Celsius than at 18 degrees Celsius. If your jars warm up under the lamp over a two hour session, the last jars are not comparable to the first. Randomise or reverse the dose order across jars so that any drift in time, temperature or operator technique does not line up with dose order.

The measurement chain matters as much as the chemistry. The US EPA guidance on generating high-quality turbidity data treats the sensor, the sample path, the calibration record and the data system as one chain, where the weakest element sets the usable resolution. The US EPA field turbidity measurement guidance sets out the practical quality control: calibration verification with a check standard before the run, matched and indexed sample cells, clean and scratch-free glass, degassing or careful pouring to avoid bubbles, and consistent time between pour and read. These are United States technical references. Your own laboratory or site procedure and your approved analytical method govern what you actually do in Ontario.

Here is a register that works as the live bench sheet.

| Jar | Target dose (mg/L as alum) | Stock strength (mg/mL) | Stock volume added (mL) | Delivered dose corrected for volume (mg/L) | pH after rapid mix | Settled turbidity, replicate set (NTU) | Mean (NTU) | Range (NTU) | Constraint flags |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 18.0 | 6.45 | 5.58 | 17.95 | 6.92 | 1.02 / 1.11 / 0.98 | 1.04 | 0.13 | pass pH |
| 2 | 22.0 | 6.45 | 6.82 | 21.93 | 6.81 | 0.74 / 0.69 / 0.78 | 0.74 | 0.09 | pass pH |
| 3 | 26.0 | 6.45 | 8.06 | 25.90 | 6.70 | 0.62 / 0.71 / 0.66 | 0.66 | 0.09 | pass pH |
| 4 | 30.0 | 6.45 | 9.30 | 29.86 | 6.55 | 0.58 / 0.61 / 0.57 | 0.59 | 0.04 | pass pH |
| 5 | 34.0 | 6.45 | 10.54 | 33.82 | 6.21 | 0.48 / 0.59 / 0.52 | 0.53 | 0.11 | fails trial pH floor |
| 6 | 38.0 | 6.45 | 11.78 | 37.78 | 5.98 | 0.44 / 0.51 / 0.47 | 0.47 | 0.07 | fails trial pH floor |

### Worked example 1: from drum strength to delivered dose

Supplied case assumptions for this teaching example only, all fictional: liquid aluminium sulphate as delivered has a density of 1.330 g/mL and is 48.5 percent by mass as alum, Al2(SO4)3 with 14 waters of hydration. Raw water alkalinity is 42 mg/L as CaCO3. Jar volume is 2.00 L. Target dose is 30.0 mg/L expressed as alum product.

Step 1, mass of alum per litre of neat product:
1.000 L product x 1000 mL/L = 1000 mL product
1000 mL x 1.330 g/mL = 1330 g product
1330 g product x 0.485 g alum/g product = 645.0 g alum per litre of product

Step 2, prepare the bench stock by diluting 10.0 mL of neat product to 1.000 L:
645.0 g alum/L x 0.0100 L = 6.450 g alum
6.450 g alum / 1.000 L = 6.450 g/L = 6450 mg/L = 6.45 mg/mL

Step 3, mass of alum required in the jar:
30.0 mg/L x 2.00 L = 60.0 mg alum

Step 4, stock volume to pipette:
60.0 mg / 6.45 mg/mL = 9.30 mL of stock

Step 5, correct for the volume you just added:
final volume = 2.000 L + 0.00930 L = 2.0093 L
delivered dose = 60.0 mg / 2.0093 L = 29.86 mg/L as alum
error against target = (30.0 - 29.86) / 30.0 x 100 = 0.47 percent

Step 6, restate the dose on the aluminium basis, because plant records and supplier data sheets often differ:
molar mass of Al2(SO4)3 with 14 waters = 594.4 g/mol
mass of Al per mole = 2 x 26.98 g/mol = 53.96 g/mol
Al fraction = 53.96 / 594.4 = 0.0908 g Al per g alum
29.86 mg/L as alum x 0.0908 = 2.71 mg/L as Al

Step 7, estimate alkalinity consumption using the textbook stoichiometric factor for this hydrate, 0.505 mg alkalinity as CaCO3 consumed per mg of alum:
29.86 mg/L x 0.505 = 15.1 mg/L as CaCO3 consumed
42 mg/L - 15.1 mg/L = 26.9 mg/L as CaCO3 remaining

Answer: pipette 9.30 mL of 6.45 mg/mL stock into a 2.00 L jar to deliver 29.86 mg/L as alum, equal to 2.71 mg/L as Al, with an estimated residual alkalinity of about 26.9 mg/L as CaCO3 in this fictional case.

The judgment point is step 5 and step 6. A 0.47 percent volume error is trivial. If you had used a weak 500 mg/L stock you would have added 120 mL to a 2.00 L jar, a 6 percent dilution of the raw water itself, which changes raw turbidity and alkalinity across jars in proportion to dose. That is a confounded run. Conversely, a very strong stock forces you to pipette under 1 mL, where pipette error becomes the dominant variability. Choose a stock strength that keeps additions in roughly the 2 mL to 15 mL range for a 2 L jar, and record it.

### Worked example 2: is the difference between two doses bigger than the bench noise

Supplied case assumptions, fictional day 1 run: raw water 8.4 NTU at 6 degrees Celsius. Dose A is 26 mg/L as alum with independently dosed triplicate jars reading 0.62, 0.71 and 0.66 NTU settled. Dose B is 34 mg/L with triplicate jars reading 0.48, 0.59 and 0.52 NTU settled.

Step 1, means:
A: (0.62 + 0.71 + 0.66) NTU / 3 = 1.99 NTU / 3 = 0.6633 NTU
B: (0.48 + 0.59 + 0.52) NTU / 3 = 1.59 NTU / 3 = 0.5300 NTU
difference = 0.6633 NTU - 0.5300 NTU = 0.1333 NTU

Step 2, sample variance for A:
deviations = -0.0433, +0.0467, -0.0033 NTU
squares = 0.001875 + 0.002178 + 0.000011 = 0.004064 NTU squared
variance = 0.004064 / (3 - 1) = 0.002032 NTU squared
standard deviation = 0.0451 NTU

Step 3, sample variance for B:
deviations = -0.0500, +0.0600, -0.0100 NTU
squares = 0.002500 + 0.003600 + 0.000100 = 0.006200 NTU squared
variance = 0.006200 / 2 = 0.003100 NTU squared
standard deviation = 0.0557 NTU

Step 4, pooled repeatability standard deviation:
pooled variance = (0.002032 + 0.003100) / 2 = 0.002566 NTU squared
pooled standard deviation = 0.0507 NTU

Step 5, standard error of the difference:
0.0507 NTU x square root of (1/3 + 1/3) = 0.0507 x 0.8165 = 0.0414 NTU

Step 6, least significant difference at 95 percent confidence with 4 degrees of freedom, t = 2.776:
2.776 x 0.0414 NTU = 0.115 NTU

Step 7, compare:
observed difference 0.1333 NTU is greater than 0.115 NTU

Answer for day 1: the 0.133 NTU improvement from Dose A to Dose B is larger than the run repeatability can explain at 95 percent confidence in this fictional data set.

Now the second half of the judgment. Supplied fictional day 2 run, raw water 4.1 NTU at 9 degrees Celsius, same procedure: Dose A reads 0.55, 0.60 and 0.58 NTU, mean = 1.73 / 3 = 0.5767 NTU. Dose B reads 0.56, 0.62 and 0.57 NTU, mean = 1.75 / 3 = 0.5833 NTU. Difference = 0.5767 - 0.5833 = -0.0067 NTU, which is far inside the pooled repeatability computed above.

So the day 1 result was repeatable within the session and did not reproduce across sessions. The correct written conclusion is that the benefit of the higher dose appears conditional on higher raw turbidity and colder water in this fictional pair of runs, and that a causal treatment conclusion is not supported by two runs on two waters. One more caution: 0.115 NTU is close to the practical resolution of many bench turbidimeters near 0.5 NTU. If your check standard tolerance and cell to cell bias, documented per your site procedure and consistent with the US EPA field turbidity measurement guidance, are wider than the least significant difference, the statistics are describing instrument behaviour, not coagulation.

### Screening candidates against the stated constraints

Lowest settled turbidity does not win by default. Score every candidate against every stated criterion and record the criterion source beside it. The criteria below are fictional trial screening values chosen for this example, not regulatory limits and not authorized setpoints.

| Criterion (fictional trial value) | Basis in this example | Dose 26 mg/L | Dose 30 mg/L | Dose 34 mg/L |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Settled turbidity at or below 0.80 NTU | bench screening target | 0.66, pass | 0.59, pass | 0.53, pass |
| Coagulation pH 6.3 to 6.8 after rapid mix | plant validated operating band | 6.70, pass | 6.55, pass | 6.21, fail |
| Residual alkalinity at or above 20 mg/L as CaCO3 | finished water stability target | 28.9, pass | 26.9, pass | 24.8, pass |
| Estimated Al carryover acceptable | plant historical correlation | pass | pass | not assessed |
| No change required to downstream pH correction | run constraint | pass | pass | fail, caustic required |
| Overall | | candidate | preferred candidate | rejected under stated constraints |

Dose 34 mg/L gave the lowest settled turbidity and is still rejected, because it breaches the stated pH band and would only work with an added base dose that was not part of the tested condition. Adding caustic creates a different experiment that must be run as such, with the base dose recorded as its own variable.

The pH consequence reaches further than the clarifier. Coagulation pH shifts the pH of water arriving at the disinfection contactor. The Ontario Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water treats CT as condition specific, depending on the disinfectant, temperature, pH, measured residual and the approved hydraulic basis such as T10 for the specific contactor configuration. A coagulation change that moves pH therefore touches disinfection performance and must be evaluated against the facility approval and the approved CT basis, not assumed to be an improvement because free chlorine is generally more effective at lower pH.

### Common errors

First error: calling three readings of one jar a triplicate. This understates variability, sometimes by a factor of three or more, which makes the least significant difference artificially small and lets you declare a dose difference that does not exist. Independently dosed jars or nothing.

Second error: reporting only the mean. A mean of 0.60 NTU from 0.55 and 0.65 NTU is evidence of a settled, controlled bench method. The same mean from 0.10 and 1.10 NTU is evidence that something in the procedure is out of control, most often floc disturbance while sampling the supernatant or an uncontrolled settling time. Always carry the individual values and the range beside the mean.

Third error: using a weak stock solution so that high-dose jars receive a much larger volume of dilution water than low-dose jars. Dose and dilution then move together and you cannot separate them. Check the added volume as a percentage of jar volume and keep it small and roughly similar across jars.

Fourth error: skipping the calibration verification because the instrument "was fine yesterday", then reporting differences of 0.1 NTU. Without a pre-run check standard result on the bench sheet, the numbers cannot be defended.

Fifth error: writing "optimum dose" on the sheet. Bench work identifies a candidate for further evaluation. Anything stronger invites someone to change the plant on the strength of six jars.

### What to verify before you act

Before a bench candidate influences anything at full scale, check these specific documents and records, not memory. The facility Drinking Water Works Permit and Municipal Drinking Water Licence, including the approved process description and any chemical or dose conditions. The Environmental Compliance Approval or equivalent approval instrument that governs the treatment train. The plant operational plan and the documented procedure for coagulant dose changes, including who may authorize a change, the required monitoring during the change and the rollback trigger. The approved CT basis and the Ontario Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water for anything that shifts pH, temperature effects or contact conditions. The laboratory or site analytical procedure and calibration records for the turbidimeter used, consistent with the quality control expectations described in the US EPA field turbidity measurement guidance and the US EPA guidance on generating high-quality turbidity data, both of which are United States technical references rather than Ontario law. Finally, confirm your own authority under O. Reg. 128/04, which sets out operator designation, duties and record requirements at sections 23 and 25 to 27. A bench result never overrides the designation and authorization structure.

### Records, wording and scale-up

Retain the raw bench sheet with individual replicate values, not a typed summary. Retain the stock preparation record including product lot, density or assay used, dilution made and date prepared, because stock strength drift is a common hidden cause of a run that will not reproduce. Retain the pre-run and post-run calibration verification results and the instrument identifier. Retain raw water characterisation at the time of sampling: turbidity, pH, alkalinity, temperature and any relevant organics indicator. Retain the mixing and settling parameters used. If any jar was disturbed, spilled, mis-dosed or read late, record it and keep the value with a note instead of deleting it.

Word the conclusion so it survives review. A defensible sentence looks like this: "Under the stated bench conditions on the fictional dates shown, 30 mg/L as alum is a candidate for further evaluation. It met the trial pH band and the settled turbidity screening value, with a replicate range of 0.04 NTU. The higher 34 mg/L candidate produced lower settled turbidity but fell outside the trial pH band and is rejected without a paired base dose trial. The dose effect observed at high raw turbidity did not reproduce at lower raw turbidity, so no causal treatment conclusion is drawn. Scale-up requires authorization under the facility approval and an approved trial protocol with defined monitoring and rollback."

When a condition changes, the decision changes. Colder water usually needs longer flocculation before settled turbidity means anything, so a fixed 20 minute settling time may misrank doses in winter. Higher raw organics shift the dose needed for charge neutralisation upward and pull coagulation pH down harder. A coagulant product change, even the same chemical from a different supplier, changes the density and assay and therefore the stock strength calculation in worked example 1. A turbidimeter swap changes the resolution assumption in worked example 2. In each case, rerun the bench comparison rather than reusing the old conclusion.
modules.evidence:
### Fictional worked scenario

All facilities, operators, records and readings below are fictional and are used only for training. No value here is an authorized setpoint or a regulatory limit.

**Setting.** Maple Hollow Water Treatment Plant, fictional. Operator M. Trudel runs a six-jar comparison on 14 February. Raw water: 9.6 NTU, pH 7.68, alkalinity 44 mg/L as CaCO3, 4 degrees Celsius. Bench stock recorded as 6450 mg/L as alum, that is 6.45 mg/mL. Jar volume 2.00 L. Fictional trial screening criteria for this run: settled turbidity at or below 0.80 NTU and coagulation pH between 6.3 and 6.8.

**Supplied bench sheet.**

| Jar | Recorded dose (mg/L) | Stock added (mL) | pH after mix | Settled turbidity (NTU) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 22.0 | 6.82 | 6.79 | 0.74 / 0.69 / 0.78 |
| B | 30.0 | 9.30 | 6.55 | 0.58 / 0.61 / 0.57 |
| C | 38.0 | 6.00 | not recorded | 0.21 (single jar) |

Handwritten note on the sheet: "38 mg/L confirmed optimum, set full scale to 38."

**Solution.**

Check Jar C against the stock record:
6.00 mL x 6.45 mg/mL = 38.7 mg alum
38.7 mg / 2.00 L = 19.35 mg/L as alum

The recorded 38.0 mg/L is unsupported. The jar actually received about 19.4 mg/L, roughly half the labelled dose. The 0.21 NTU result also breaks the trend set by Jars A and B, where turbidity falls as dose rises, which is a second independent flag that the jar or the reading is wrong. Jar C has no replicate and no pH entry, so it cannot be screened against the pH criterion at all. Reject Jar C and the handwritten conclusion.

Verify the two usable jars:
Jar A: (0.74 + 0.69 + 0.78) / 3 = 2.21 / 3 = 0.7367 NTU, range 0.09 NTU
Jar B: (0.58 + 0.61 + 0.57) / 3 = 1.76 / 3 = 0.5867 NTU, range 0.04 NTU
difference = 0.7367 - 0.5867 = 0.1500 NTU

Alkalinity check on Jar B using the stoichiometric factor 0.505 mg as CaCO3 per mg alum:
30.0 mg/L x 0.505 = 15.2 mg/L as CaCO3
44 - 15.2 = 28.8 mg/L as CaCO3 remaining

**Conclusion to record.** Jar B at 30.0 mg/L as alum is a candidate for further evaluation: it met both fictional trial criteria with a replicate range of 0.04 NTU. Jar C is void and must be rerun with correct stock volume, triplicate jars and a pH reading. No dose change may be made at full scale on this evidence.

checks.prompt: In a bench jar session, an operator reads the same cuvette three times and logs the three values as replicates. What does that spread actually measure?
choices: Instrument noise alone, without sampling or dosing variability
Instrument noise plus sampling noise from separate aliquots
Instrument noise plus dosing and mixing variability combined
True jar to jar variability of the bench coagulation procedure
checks.explanation: Re-reading one cuvette only repeats the measurement step, so it captures turbidimeter noise. Three aliquots from one jar would add sampling noise, and only independently dosed and independently settled jars add dosing and mixing variability, so the jar to jar option overstates what this spread can show.

checks.prompt: A jar test ranks candidate doses using settled supernatant turbidity. Which statement best describes what that response variable does and does not represent?
choices: It indicates disinfection performance because turbidity shields pathogens
It proxies floc formation and settleability, not filtered water turbidity
It predicts filter run length once bench floc strength looks adequate
It measures residual aluminium carried through the settled supernatant
checks.explanation: Settled turbidity is a proxy for floc formation and settling under one fixed bench condition. Filter run length, residual aluminium and disinfection performance are separate response variables, so the filter run length option treats a bench proxy as if it predicted plant filter behaviour.

checks.prompt: Jars are dosed lowest to highest over a two hour session under a bench lamp, and sample temperature rises from 7 to 12 degrees Celsius. Why is reversing or randomising dose order recommended?
choices: So the turbidimeter can be calibrated between each dosed jar
So warmer jars flocculate faster and mask the lowest dose result
So time and temperature drift does not line up with dose order
So the highest dose always gets the longest settling period
checks.explanation: If drift in time, temperature or technique follows dose order, the apparent dose effect is confounded with that drift. Deliberately giving the highest dose the longest settling period would itself create a systematic difference other than dose, which is exactly what must be avoided.

checks.prompt: For a 2.00 L jar test with target doses from 18 to 38 mg/L as alum, which bench stock choice best limits both dilution of the raw water and pipette error?
choices: A 500 mg/L stock needing about 120 mL of addition per jar
A very strong stock needing under 1 mL of addition per jar
Neat product added directly by drops so no dilution occurs at all
A stock needing roughly 2 to 15 mL of addition per 2.00 L jar
checks.explanation: Additions in the range of a few millilitres keep the raw water dilution negligible while staying above the volume where pipette error dominates. A 120 mL addition dilutes the raw water by about 6 percent in proportion to dose, which confounds raw turbidity and alkalinity across the jars.

checks.prompt: In a fictional bench register, mean settled turbidity falls from 1.04 NTU at 18 mg/L to 0.47 NTU at 38 mg/L as alum, but the 34 and 38 mg/L jars are flagged as failing the trial pH floor. Which candidate dose is best within the stated constraints?
choices: 30 mg/L, the lowest turbidity among jars passing the pH check
38 mg/L, since it gave the lowest settled turbidity of the run
34 mg/L, since its pH flag is only marginally below the floor
18 mg/L, since the lowest dose is safest for alkalinity margin
checks.explanation: Candidate doses are compared only within the stated constraints, so flagged jars are out of contention no matter how low their turbidity reads. Choosing 38 mg/L ranks on turbidity alone and ignores the pH constraint that the trial itself defined for this fictional exercise.

checks.prompt: Two fictional jar runs use identical procedure and a fixed 20 minute settling time, one at 3 degrees Celsius and one at 18 degrees Celsius. How should the colder run be interpreted?
choices: The colder run can be compared directly if raw turbidity values match
Slower kinetics and higher viscosity penalise doses at fixed settling
Cold water floc settles faster, so the results overstate dose performance
Temperature has no effect once rapid mix energy and time are matched
checks.explanation: Cold water slows flocculation kinetics and raises viscosity, so a fixed settling time makes every dose look worse at 3 degrees Celsius. Claiming faster settling in cold water reverses the physics, and matching raw turbidity alone does not remove the temperature confounder.

modules.title: Chemical mass and actual feed delivery
objectives: Convert solution delivery to active chemical dose.
Reconcile pump indication with a measured delivery check.
modules.lesson:
### The dose basis question comes before any arithmetic

A chemical dose is meaningless until you say what it is a dose *of*. The same alum pump running at the same speed can be correctly described as 38 mg/L, 6.6 mg/L or 3.5 mg/L, and all three numbers can be right at the same time. They differ only in basis: as-supplied product, as an oxide equivalent, or as the metal. Jar test results, plant historians, coagulant cost tracking and optimization trials all collapse into nonsense when the basis is not stated and carried forward.

The bases you will meet in an Ontario drinking-water plant are these. Product basis, sometimes called as-delivered or as-supplied, is the mass of the commercial liquid or solid per volume of water treated. Active or dry-equivalent basis is the mass of the named compound in that product. Elemental or oxide basis expresses the same feed as aluminum, as Al2O3, as iron, or as available chlorine. Solution basis applies when a dry product is made down on site and reported as the diluted solution rather than the dry chemical.

The operational rule is simple. Write the basis into the same field as the number, every time, in every log, jar test sheet and trend tag. A tag named ALUM_DOSE tells the next operator nothing. A tag named ALUM_DOSE_MG_L_AS_PRODUCT does. The US EPA guidance titled Generating high-quality turbidity data makes the same point about the measurement chain for turbidity instruments: the number a control system displays is only as trustworthy as the documented chain of scaling, units and calibration behind it. That logic transfers directly to chemical feed tags.

### The core equation, with units carried

For a liquid chemical delivered by a metering pump into a known water flow:

Active mass rate (kg/h) = Solution flow (L/h) x Solution density (kg/L) x Active mass fraction (dimensionless)

Dose (mg/L) = [Active mass rate (kg/h) / Water flow (m3/h)] x 1000

The 1000 factor is not magic. 1 kg per 1 m3 equals 1 000 000 mg per 1 000 L, which is 1000 mg/L. Carry the units on every line and the factor appears on its own.

Four terms, four places to be wrong.

Solution flow must be an actual delivered volume, not a setpoint or a stroke percentage. Density must be the density of that lot at roughly the temperature in the day tank, taken from the certificate of analysis or the supplier data sheet, not assumed to be 1.00 kg/L. Active mass fraction must be a decimal, and you must know whether the supplier quoted it as weight per weight or weight per volume. Water flow must be the flow actually passing the injection point, not total plant production, and not raw flow when the chemical is dosed on a filtered side stream.

The weight per weight versus weight per volume trap is worst with sodium hypochlorite. A product sold as 12 percent available chlorine by volume contains about 120 g/L of available chlorine, and at a density near 1.20 kg/L that is roughly 10 percent by weight. If you multiply 1.20 kg/L by 0.12 you get 0.144 kg/L, which overstates the active content by about 20 percent relative to the 0.120 kg/L the product actually contains. Use the grams per litre figure when the supplier gives one, because it removes the density step entirely.

### Worked example 1: solution feed converted to three valid dose bases

Supplied case assumptions for this teaching example only. These are not authorized values for any plant.

Fictional plant, liquid aluminum sulphate. Certificate of analysis for lot 24-118 states 48.5 percent w/w alum as Al2(SO4)3 with 14 waters, 8.30 percent w/w as Al2O3, density 1.33 kg/L at 20 degrees C. Metering pump indication 12.5 L/h. Flow at the rapid mix point 210 m3/h.

Step 1, solution mass rate:
12.5 L/h x 1.33 kg/L = 16.625 kg/h of product

Step 2, active mass rate on product basis (the alum compound itself):
16.625 kg/h x 0.485 = 8.063 kg/h as Al2(SO4)3 . 14H2O

Step 3, dose on that basis:
8.063 kg/h / 210 m3/h = 0.03840 kg/m3
0.03840 kg/m3 x 1000 = 38.4 mg/L as dry alum

Step 4, same feed on the Al2O3 basis:
16.625 kg/h x 0.0830 = 1.380 kg/h as Al2O3
1.380 kg/h / 210 m3/h = 0.006571 kg/m3
0.006571 kg/m3 x 1000 = 6.57 mg/L as Al2O3

Step 5, same feed on the elemental aluminum basis. Al2O3 has a molar mass of 101.96 g/mol and contains 2 x 26.98 g/mol = 53.96 g/mol of aluminum, so the mass fraction of Al in Al2O3 is 53.96 / 101.96 = 0.5292.
6.57 mg/L x 0.5292 = 3.48 mg/L as Al

Answer: one pump setting, three correct numbers. 38.4 mg/L as dry alum, 6.57 mg/L as Al2O3, 3.48 mg/L as Al. If a jar test was run and reported as mg/L as Al and an operator enters it as mg/L as product, the plant runs at roughly one eleventh of the intended coagulant dose.

### The drawdown check: converting pump indication into measured delivery

A controller setpoint, a stroke percentage and a SCADA totaliser are all indications. None of them is a measurement of what left the pump. Diaphragm wear, air binding, a fouled foot valve, back pressure change, a partially closed isolation valve, viscosity change with tank temperature, and a scaling error in the analog output can all put indication and delivery far apart while the trend line stays perfectly smooth.

A drawdown check measures delivery directly. A graduated calibration column on the suction side is isolated from the day tank, the pump draws only from the column, and you time the fall in level. The arithmetic is:

Measured delivery (L/h) = [Volume drawn (mL) / Time (min)] x [60 min/h] / [1000 mL/L]

Deviation (%) = [(Measured L/h minus Indicated L/h) / Indicated L/h] x 100

Discipline matters more than the equation. Run the pump long enough that the timing error is small compared with the reading error. Read the meniscus at eye level. Run at least three consecutive draws at the same setpoint and report the mean and the spread, because a single draw cannot distinguish a real bias from a one-off air slug. Record tank temperature, suction and discharge pressure, stroke length and speed, and the lot number on the day tank. Do the same check at a low, mid and high setpoint if you intend to trust the pump across a range, because a pump can be accurate at 50 percent and badly off at 20 percent.

The quality-control habits described in the US EPA guidance on field turbidity measurement apply here without modification: a check is only evidence if the conditions, the instrument identity, the time and the operator are recorded with the result.

### Worked example 2: reconciliation, uncertainty and the corrected setpoint

Continuing the same fictional plant and the same lot 24-118 assumptions.

Indicated feed: 12.5 L/h. Calibration column graduated in 10 mL divisions, readable to about plus or minus 5 mL. Stopwatch resolution 1 s.

Draw 1: start 980 mL, end 224 mL, elapsed 4.00 min
Volume drawn = 980 mL minus 224 mL = 756 mL
Draw 2: 752 mL in 4.00 min
Draw 3: 754 mL in 4.00 min
Mean volume = (756 + 752 + 754) mL / 3 = 754 mL

Step 1, measured delivery:
754 mL / 4.00 min = 188.5 mL/min
188.5 mL/min x 60 min/h = 11 310 mL/h
11 310 mL/h / 1000 mL/L = 11.31 L/h

Step 2, deviation from indication:
(11.31 L/h minus 12.5 L/h) = -1.19 L/h
-1.19 L/h / 12.5 L/h x 100 = -9.5 percent

Step 3, is the deviation bigger than the measurement noise?
Volume reading uncertainty: 5 mL / 754 mL = 0.66 percent
Timing uncertainty: 1 s / 240 s = 0.42 percent
Combined by root sum of squares: square root of (0.66 squared plus 0.42 squared) = square root of (0.4356 + 0.1764) = square root of 0.6120 = 0.78 percent
Spread of the three draws: (756 minus 752) mL / 754 mL x 100 = 0.53 percent
A 9.5 percent deviation is more than ten times the combined uncertainty, so it is a real bias, not scatter.

Step 4, the dose actually being delivered:
11.31 L/h x 1.33 kg/L = 15.04 kg/h of product
15.04 kg/h x 0.485 = 7.296 kg/h as dry alum
7.296 kg/h / 210 m3/h = 0.03474 kg/m3
0.03474 kg/m3 x 1000 = 34.7 mg/L as dry alum

Step 5, the shortfall against what the operator believed:
38.4 mg/L minus 34.7 mg/L = 3.7 mg/L as dry alum, a 9.5 percent shortfall.

Step 6, indication required to actually deliver 12.5 L/h, if the site procedure permits a setpoint correction rather than a mechanical repair:
Correction factor = 12.5 L/h indicated / 11.31 L/h measured = 1.105
12.5 L/h x 1.105 = 13.81 L/h indicated

Answer: the pump is delivering 11.31 L/h against an indication of 12.5 L/h, a bias of -9.5 percent, giving an actual dose of 34.7 mg/L as dry alum instead of the assumed 38.4 mg/L. An indicated 13.8 L/h would restore the intended delivery, but only if the resulting dose stays inside the range the plant is approved and validated to run, and only if the root cause has been identified and recorded rather than masked.

### Input register and deviation decision table

Use a register like this before any dose calculation. Every value needs a named source and a date, or it does not get used.

| Term | Value used | Units | Source of value | Verified by and date | Expires or recheck when |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Product name and lot | Liquid alum, lot 24-118 | text | Bill of lading, day tank label | Operator, delivery date | New delivery to day tank |
| Density | 1.33 | kg/L at 20 C | Certificate of analysis | Operator, delivery date | Lot change or tank temp shift |
| Active fraction, product basis | 0.485 | w/w | Certificate of analysis | Operator, delivery date | Lot change |
| Active fraction, Al2O3 basis | 0.0830 | w/w | Certificate of analysis | Operator, delivery date | Lot change |
| Indicated feed | 12.5 | L/h | SCADA tag and local display | Operator, shift | Each shift reading |
| Measured feed | 11.31 | L/h | Drawdown, 3 draws, 4.00 min | Operator, test date | Per site calibration frequency |
| Water flow at injection | 210 | m3/h | Flow meter, last calibration on file | Operator, shift | Meter calibration interval |
| Dose basis reported | as dry alum | text | Site procedure | Supervisor | Procedure revision |

The acceptance bands below are an example drawn from a fictional site calibration procedure. They are not a general standard. Your own approval, operations manual and calibration procedure set the bands that apply to you.

| Measured versus indicated deviation | Interpretation | Example action under the fictional site procedure |
|---|---|---|
| Within the combined measurement uncertainty | No detectable bias | Record result, no change |
| Small but repeatable bias, consistent across three draws | Real bias, drift or scaling offset | Record, notify the overall responsible operator, schedule correction |
| Large bias, or measured delivery near zero | Suspect air lock, foot valve, diaphragm or closed valve | Do not chase it with setpoint changes, investigate mechanically, verify residual or turbidity response |
| Measured exceeds indicated | Suspect siphoning, low back pressure, or scaling error | Check discharge back pressure and anti-siphon device before adjusting |
| Draws disagree with each other by more than the spread the procedure allows | Test is not valid | Repeat after purging air and re-verifying isolation |

### Common errors

Treating a percentage as a whole number. Entering 48.5 instead of 0.485 inflates the answer one hundredfold. The check is a sanity comparison: a coagulant dose of 3840 mg/L is not a plausible drinking-water number, and the operator who does not pause at that result has stopped reading their own output.

Assuming density 1.00 kg/L. Liquid alum near 1.33 kg/L, ferric chloride near 1.4 kg/L and 12 percent hypochlorite near 1.2 kg/L are all significantly denser than water. Using 1.00 understates alum active mass by roughly 25 percent relative to the correct calculation. The density belongs to the lot and to the temperature, so a cold day tank in February is not the same as the 20 degrees C figure on the certificate.

Using a pump curve or calibration result from a different product or a different concentration. A curve relates stroke and speed to volumetric delivery for a given fluid. It says nothing about active mass if the concentration changed at the last delivery, and it may not even hold volumetrically if the new product has a different viscosity.

Calling one drawdown a calibration. A single draw cannot separate a genuine bias from an air slug or a misread meniscus. Three draws with the spread recorded is the minimum that lets you defend the number.

Mixing the flow basis. Dividing by total plant flow when the chemical is injected into one of two parallel trains overstates the water being dosed and understates the true dose in that train.

### What to verify before you act

Verify the Drinking Water Works Permit and the Municipal Drinking Water Licence, and the Environmental Compliance Approval terms that apply to your works, for the chemicals approved for use, the approved points of application and any dose or feed constraints written into those instruments. A calculation never authorizes a chemical, a feed point or a dose range.

Verify the site operations manual and the standard operating procedure for calibration column drawdown, including isolation, personal protective equipment, spill response, venting and the requirement for a second person. The arithmetic in this module does not authorize opening a chemical line. If the procedure does not cover the test you intend to run, you do not run it.

Verify the certificate of analysis for the lot currently in the day tank, not the previous one, and confirm whether the active fraction is quoted weight per weight, weight per volume or grams per litre.

Verify your authority under O. Reg. 128/04, sections 23 and 25 to 27, which deal with designation, operator duties and records. Adjusting a chemical feed is an operating decision that must be made by a person with the authority to make it, communicated to the overall responsible operator, and recorded.

Where the chemical is a primary disinfectant, verify the Ontario Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water and the disinfection requirements in your approval before changing feed. CT is condition specific. It depends on the disinfectant, temperature, pH, measured residual and the approved hydraulic basis for that contactor, so a feed change is never a standalone decision.

Retain as evidence: the raw drawdown sheet with start and end volumes, times, number of draws and operator initials; the indicated setpoint and stroke settings; the water flow and its source; the certificate of analysis; the tank temperature; the calculation with units shown; the deviation and the conclusion; and the notification made to the overall responsible operator. A corrected setpoint with no retained calculation is an undocumented change.
modules.evidence:
### Fictional worked scenario

**All facilities, operators, records and readings below are fictional and are used for training only. None of the values are authorized operating values for any real plant.**

Mapleford Water Treatment Plant, fictional, conventional filtration, single train. Coagulant is liquid alum. Day tank filled from delivery lot 25-042.

Supplied records:
- Certificate of analysis, lot 25-042: 49.2 percent w/w alum, density 1.335 kg/L at 20 degrees C.
- SCADA indication for coagulant pump P-201: 15.0 L/h at 62 percent stroke.
- Plant flow at rapid mix: 185 m3/h, meter calibrated within the interval on file.
- Laminated pump curve taped to the panel, undated, marked "62 percent equals 15.0 L/h", issued for a previous product.
- Handwritten note in the shift binder, unsigned: "alum is 10 percent, density 1.0, just use 1.5 kg/h."
- Drawdown check by the operator, calibration column isolated per the site procedure, three draws: 916 mL, 918 mL and 920 mL, each over 5.00 min.

Records the learner must reject: the unsigned handwritten note, because it contradicts the certificate of analysis for the lot in the tank and has no source or signature; and the undated pump curve, because it was issued for a different product and is superseded by the measured drawdown.

Solution:

Mean volume drawn = (916 + 918 + 920) mL / 3 = 918 mL
918 mL / 5.00 min = 183.6 mL/min
183.6 mL/min x 60 min/h = 11 016 mL/h
11 016 mL/h / 1000 mL/L = 11.02 L/h measured

Deviation = (11.02 L/h minus 15.0 L/h) / 15.0 L/h x 100 = -26.5 percent
Spread of draws = (920 minus 916) mL / 918 mL x 100 = 0.44 percent, so the bias is real.

Actual dose:
11.02 L/h x 1.335 kg/L = 14.71 kg/h product
14.71 kg/h x 0.492 = 7.238 kg/h as dry alum
7.238 kg/h / 185 m3/h = 0.03913 kg/m3 = 39.1 mg/L as dry alum

Dose the operator believed was being fed:
15.0 L/h x 1.335 kg/L x 0.492 = 9.854 kg/h
9.854 kg/h / 185 m3/h = 0.05327 kg/m3 = 53.3 mg/L as dry alum
Shortfall = 53.3 minus 39.1 = 14.2 mg/L as dry alum.

The rejected note would have given 15.0 L/h x 1.0 kg/L x 0.10 = 1.5 kg/h, or 8.1 mg/L, which is wrong by a factor of about five against the measured delivery.

Action: report the measured bias to the overall responsible operator, record the drawdown sheet, certificate of analysis, flow source and calculation, remove the superseded pump curve and the unsigned note from the panel and binder, and treat the pump as requiring mechanical investigation rather than a setpoint correction until the cause is identified. Any dose change must stay within the plant approval and the site procedure.

Read the source sections and note one application limit.

checks.prompt: At a fictional plant, one alum metering pump setting is logged as 38.4 mg/L, 6.57 mg/L and 3.48 mg/L on the same shift. What makes all three numbers correct at the same time?
choices: All three state the same feed on product, oxide and metal bases.
The pump drifted between three readings taken during that shift.
Three different water flow values were used in the dose equation.
Density was corrected for tank temperature in only one of them.
checks.explanation: One feed rate can be expressed as dry alum product, as Al2O3, or as elemental Al, so the basis must be written beside the number. Pump drift is a tempting answer but drift would not produce a fixed ratio between the three values, and these three are related only by mass fractions.

checks.prompt: Supplied case assumptions for practice only: a pump delivers 10.0 L/h of coagulant, density 1.30 kg/L, 50.0 percent w/w active, into 200 m3/h measured at the injection point. What is the dose on the active basis?
choices: 3.25 mg/L as active chemical
32.5 mg/L as active chemical
25.0 mg/L as active chemical
65.0 mg/L as active chemical
checks.explanation: 10.0 L/h x 1.30 kg/L = 13.0 kg/h product, x 0.500 = 6.50 kg/h active, divided by 200 m3/h = 0.0325 kg/m3, x 1000 = 32.5 mg/L. The 25.0 mg/L answer comes from skipping density and assuming 1.00 kg/L, which understates the true feed.

checks.prompt: A dose calculation for a fictional plant used 1.00 kg/L for a liquid alum whose certificate of analysis states 1.33 kg/L at 20 degrees C. What is the effect on the calculated dose?
choices: It has no effect because density cancels in the equation.
It changes the reported basis but not the dose value.
It understates the delivered dose by roughly 25 percent.
It overstates the delivered dose by roughly 33 percent.
checks.explanation: The calculated mass rate is scaled by 1.00/1.33 = 0.752, so the figure is about 25 percent low and the plant is actually feeding more than the log shows. Density does not cancel, because solution flow is volumetric while dose depends on mass of active chemical.

checks.prompt: A sodium hypochlorite drum is labelled 12 percent available chlorine by volume and the supplier data sheet lists density 1.20 kg/L. Which active content figure should the dose calculation use?
choices: Use 0.144 kg/L, found as 1.20 kg/L times 0.12.
Use 0.132 kg/L, the average of the two available figures.
Use 0.100 kg/L, because weight percent is always lower.
Use 120 g/L, which is the labelled volumetric strength.
checks.explanation: A volumetric percentage already includes the volume, so 12 percent by volume is about 120 g/L and no density step is needed. Multiplying 1.20 kg/L by 0.12 treats a weight per volume figure as weight per weight and overstates active content by roughly 20 percent.

checks.prompt: During a drawdown check at a fictional plant, the calibration column level falls 600 mL in 3.00 min while the pump indicates 13.0 L/h. What is the measured delivery and the deviation from indication?
choices: 12.0 L/h measured, deviation about -7.7 percent
12.0 L/h measured, deviation about -8.3 percent
12.0 L/h measured, deviation about -1.0 percent
0.20 L/h measured, deviation about -98 percent
checks.explanation: 600 mL / 3.00 min = 200 mL/min, x 60 = 12 000 mL/h = 12.0 L/h. Deviation is (12.0 minus 13.0) / 13.0 x 100 = -7.7 percent. The -8.3 percent option divides by the measured value instead of the indicated value, which is the wrong denominator for deviation from indication.

checks.prompt: Why does a defensible drawdown procedure call for at least three consecutive draws at the same setpoint, with tank temperature, suction and discharge pressure, stroke settings and day tank lot number recorded?
choices: It is required because the column cannot be refilled between draws.
It separates a real bias from one-off scatter and documents conditions.
It guarantees that averaging removes any diaphragm pump bias entirely.
It is needed because a single draw always reads low on a metering pump.
checks.explanation: Repeat draws give a spread that can be compared with the deviation, and recorded conditions make the result usable evidence later. Averaging does not remove bias; it only reduces random scatter, so a biased pump stays biased no matter how many draws are averaged.

modules.lesson:
### What the individual filter record is for

An individual filter record exists so that each unit can be judged on its own behaviour. A plant-wide number tells you what the system produced. A per-unit number tells you which unit produced it, and whether that unit is drifting, media-fouled, hydraulically starved, over-loaded, or simply being measured badly. Those are different problems with different corrective actions, and you cannot separate them from a combined value.

Four data streams make the record useful, and they are only useful together: filtrate flow, effective filter area, headloss, and filtered water turbidity, each time-stamped and each tied to run age and backwash history. Add the instrument verification history and you can defend a decision. Drop any one of them and you are guessing.

Ontario Regulation 128/04 deals with designation of the overall responsible operator and operators in charge, the duties attached to those roles, and record keeping duties in sections 23 and 25 to 27. Read the current text of those sections for your own system rather than working from memory, because they define who is permitted to make and direct operating adjustments and what has to be written down. Your facility drinking water works permit, Environmental Compliance Approval and approved operating procedures define the monitoring locations, performance criteria, alarm setpoints and reporting pathways. This module teaches how to calculate and interpret. It does not set any limit for your plant.

### Hydraulic loading rate, calculated per unit

Hydraulic loading rate is filtrate flow divided by the effective filter area of that unit:

Loading rate (m/h) = flow (m³/h) ÷ effective area (m²)

The units reduce cleanly. m³/h ÷ m² gives m³/(m²·h), which is m/h. Some design documents and United States technical guidance use L/(m²·s) or gpm/ft², so confirm which basis your approval and design drawings use before you compare a calculated value to a design figure.

Effective area is the wetted plan area of the media, taken from the as-built drawings, not from a nominal box dimension and not from a logsheet header that nobody has verified. Wall thickness, launder footprint and any partition change the number. If two filters in the same gallery are recorded with the same area and the drawings disagree, the drawings win until an engineering record says otherwise.

### Worked example 1: unequal split and the loss of the plant average

Supplied case assumptions for this example only. Fictional plant, four declining rate filters, each with effective media area of 4.0 m by 6.0 m taken from the as-built drawings. Total filtered water production is 320 m³/h. Individual filtrate flow meters read F1 95 m³/h, F2 92 m³/h, F3 48 m³/h, F4 85 m³/h.

Step 1. Effective area of one filter.
Area = 4.0 m × 6.0 m = 24.0 m²

Step 2. Total area in service.
Total area = 4 filters × 24.0 m²/filter = 96.0 m²

Step 3. Plant average loading rate.
Average loading = 320 m³/h ÷ 96.0 m² = 3.33 m³/(m²·h) = 3.33 m/h

Step 4. Individual loading rates.
F1 = 95 m³/h ÷ 24.0 m² = 3.96 m/h
F2 = 92 m³/h ÷ 24.0 m² = 3.83 m/h
F3 = 48 m³/h ÷ 24.0 m² = 2.00 m/h
F4 = 85 m³/h ÷ 24.0 m² = 3.54 m/h

Step 5. Check the sum.
95 + 92 + 48 + 85 = 320 m³/h, which matches plant production, so the individual meters are at least internally consistent with the total.

Step 6. Express F1 in an alternative unit for comparison to a design sheet.
3.96 m³/(m²·h) × 1000 L/m³ ÷ 3600 s/h = 1.10 L/(m²·s)

Answer. Plant average loading is 3.33 m/h, but the four units are running between 2.00 m/h and 3.96 m/h. F1 is carrying 19 percent more loading than the average, and F3 is carrying 40 percent less.

Step 7. What changes when a condition changes. Take F3 out of service for backwash while production is held at 320 m³/h.
Area in service = 3 filters × 24.0 m² = 72.0 m²
Average loading = 320 m³/h ÷ 72.0 m² = 4.44 m/h
If the split stays proportional to the previous flows of the three remaining units (95 + 92 + 85 = 272 m³/h), F1 receives:
F1 flow = 320 m³/h × (95 ÷ 272) = 111.8 m³/h
F1 loading = 111.8 m³/h ÷ 24.0 m² = 4.66 m/h

That is a 18 percent step increase on a single unit, applied at the same moment that a freshly backwashed filter is about to return in its ripening phase. Whether 4.66 m/h is acceptable depends entirely on the loading basis in your design documents, drinking water works permit and approved procedures. The operator judgment point is that the increase is real, it lands unevenly, and it is invisible in the plant average.

Removing a filter from service also changes flow through downstream contact chambers. The Ontario Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water explains that CT is condition specific and depends on disinfectant, temperature, pH, residual and the approved hydraulic basis, including the T10 value used for that configuration. If a filter outage forces a production change, confirm the disinfection calculation against the approved basis for the configuration you are actually running.

### Headloss trend, normalized headloss, and unit filter run volume

Headloss on its own is a number. Headloss rate is a trend, and trends are what let you compare units.

Headloss rate (m/h) = (headloss now − headloss at run start) ÷ elapsed run time (h)

A raw rate is not comparable between filters running at different loadings, because a filter taking more water collects more solids per hour. Normalize it:

Specific headloss development (m per m of applied water) = headloss rate (m/h) ÷ loading rate (m/h)

The units divide out to metres of headloss per metre of water applied, which is a clean basis for comparing units, and for comparing this run to the same unit last month at a different flow.

Unit filter run volume is the other comparison that survives a loading change:

UFRV (m³/m²) = loading rate (m/h) × run length (h)

### Worked example 2: two filters, opposite conclusions

Supplied case assumptions for this example only, same fictional plant. F1 headloss was 0.35 m at 02:00 at run start and 0.98 m at 14:00. F3 headloss was 0.30 m at 02:00 and 0.66 m at 14:00. Loading rates are the values from Example 1. The plant operating procedure for this fictional facility uses a terminal headloss assumption of 2.40 m and a maximum run length assumption of 96 h.

Step 1. Elapsed run time for both units.
Elapsed = 14:00 − 02:00 = 12 h

Step 2. F1 headloss rate.
Δ headloss = 0.98 m − 0.35 m = 0.63 m
Rate = 0.63 m ÷ 12 h = 0.0525 m/h

Step 3. F3 headloss rate.
Δ headloss = 0.66 m − 0.30 m = 0.36 m
Rate = 0.36 m ÷ 12 h = 0.0300 m/h

Step 4. Normalize each to its loading.
F1 = 0.0525 m/h ÷ 3.96 m/h = 0.0133 m per m applied
F3 = 0.0300 m/h ÷ 2.00 m/h = 0.0150 m per m applied

Step 5. Interpret. The raw rates say F1 is clogging 75 percent faster. The normalized values say F3 is collecting about 13 percent more headloss per unit volume of water filtered. F1 is busier. F3 is dirtier per litre. If you were ranking units for a media inspection, the raw rate points at the wrong filter.

Step 6. Project F1 to the terminal headloss assumption.
Available headloss = 2.40 m − 0.98 m = 1.42 m
Time remaining = 1.42 m ÷ 0.0525 m/h = 27.0 h
Projected total run = 12 h + 27.0 h = 39.0 h

Step 7. F1 unit filter run volume at that projected run length.
UFRV = 3.96 m/h × 39.0 h = 154 m³/m²

Answer. F1 is projected to reach the assumed terminal headloss at about 39 h of run age, well inside the 96 h maximum run assumption, at a unit filter run volume near 154 m³/m². F3 normalizes worse and should be flagged for media and underdrain review even though its headloss trend looks gentler.

Step 8. What invalidates the projection. Linear projection assumes stable loading, stable coagulant dose and stable raw water. If the split changes, if coagulant dose or polymer changes, if raw water turbidity or temperature moves, or if the filter is rate-controlled and the valve position shifts, the projection is void and you recalculate from a fresh baseline. Record the reason for the reset.

### How combined data conceal unit behaviour

A combined filtered water value is a mixed stream. Mixing is flow weighted, not arithmetic:

Combined value = Σ (flow × value) ÷ Σ flow

Supplied case assumptions for this example only. Same four flows. Individual filtered turbidities read F1 0.06 NTU, F2 0.08 NTU, F3 0.35 NTU, F4 0.07 NTU.

Numerator terms:
95 m³/h × 0.06 NTU = 5.70 m³·NTU/h
92 m³/h × 0.08 NTU = 7.36 m³·NTU/h
48 m³/h × 0.35 NTU = 16.80 m³·NTU/h
85 m³/h × 0.07 NTU = 5.95 m³·NTU/h
Sum = 35.81 m³·NTU/h
Combined = 35.81 m³·NTU/h ÷ 320 m³/h = 0.112 NTU, which rounds to 0.11 NTU
Arithmetic average = (0.06 + 0.08 + 0.35 + 0.07) NTU ÷ 4 = 0.56 NTU ÷ 4 = 0.14 NTU

Answer. The combined stream is near 0.11 NTU while one unit sits at 0.35 NTU. The arithmetic average of 0.14 NTU is not the mixed value, and in this case it happens to be higher than the true mix because the poor performer is also the low flow unit. Reverse the flows and the same arithmetic average would understate the mix. This is a training approximation that explains dilution. It is not a substitute for the individual filter monitoring your approval and the applicable regulation require, and it is never a basis for reporting.

### Daily individual filter register and troubleshooting matrix

Use a register that forces every comparison to be made on the same page. Blank cells are the signal that a judgment was made without data.

| Filter | Effective area (m²) | Filtrate flow (m³/h) | Loading (m/h) | HL start (m) | HL now (m) | Run age (h) | HL rate (m/h) | Specific HL (m/m) | Turbidity (NTU) | Ripening peak (NTU) and duration | Analyser verified (date) | Flag |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | 24.0 | 95 | 3.96 | 0.35 | 0.98 | 12 | 0.0525 | 0.0133 | 0.06 | 0.18 / 9 min | 2 days ago | none |
| F2 | 24.0 | 92 | 3.83 | 0.33 | 0.90 | 12 | 0.0475 | 0.0124 | 0.08 | 0.21 / 11 min | 2 days ago | none |
| F3 | 24.0 | 48 | 2.00 | 0.30 | 0.66 | 12 | 0.0300 | 0.0150 | 0.35 | 0.62 / 34 min | 26 days ago | review |
| F4 | 24.0 | 85 | 3.54 | 0.31 | 0.84 | 12 | 0.0442 | 0.0125 | 0.07 | 0.19 / 8 min | 2 days ago | none |

| Observed pattern | Process causes to test | Measurement causes to test | First checks | Evidence to retain |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| One unit high turbidity, normal headloss trend | Short circuiting, media loss, underdrain or gravel disturbance, cracked media bed | Fouled optics, air bubbles, low sample line flow, calibration drift | Sample line flow rate, bubble trap, grab sample by approved bench method, visual bed inspection at backwash | Grab comparison result, verification record, photos, bed profile notes |
| Headloss trend flat while turbidity rises | Bed cracking or mudball formation with wall short circuit | Transmitter stuck, SCADA hold or frozen tag, failed scaling | Compare transmitter to local gauge, check tag update timestamp | Trend export, local gauge reading, instrument work order |
| All units drift up together | Coagulation upset, dose or pH out of range, raw water change | Common reference standard or bench instrument error | Jar test, raw water parameters, streaming current or zeta trend | Jar test sheet, dose records, raw water log |
| Headloss rate doubles with no turbidity change | Loading step after unit removal, overdose, polymer change | Flow meter drift changing the loading denominator | Recalculate loading from verified flow, confirm valve position | Flow verification, valve log, dose change log |
| Long or high ripening peak on one unit | Inadequate backwash, media fines, filter to waste too short | Analyser lag, sample transport delay | Backwash flow and duration records, transport time estimate | Backwash record, ripening trend, analyser response check |

### Measurement chain and data quality

The reading you act on is the output of a chain: sample tap location, sample line, flow through the line, bubble removal, the analyser optics and light source, the calibration and verification history, the signal scaling, and the data historian. United States technical guidance in Generating high-quality turbidity data and in Field turbidity measurement describes this chain and the quality control steps that protect it, including verification against reference material, control of stray light and bubbles, sample handling and documentation of corrective action. Those documents are technical guidance, not Ontario law. Your bench or on-line method must be the one named in your approved procedure and sampling plan.

Invalidating conditions you should be able to name on the spot: sample line flow outside the analyser manufacturer stated range, air entrainment, biofilm or scale on the optical window, a verification that is overdue under your procedure, a scaling mismatch between transmitter and historian, a stuck tag with an unchanged timestamp, and a sample point that is not the one named in your approval.

Never clear an alarm because it is inconvenient. Preserve it, verify under the approved procedure, and document both the process evidence and the instrument evidence. A false alarm is a conclusion supported by records, not an opinion.

### Common errors

Using nominal box dimensions instead of drawing area. A filter recorded as 25 m² when the drawings show 24.0 m² produces a loading rate about 4 percent low. That is enough to hide a unit that has crossed a design basis, and it corrupts every normalized comparison built on it.

Comparing raw headloss rates between units at different flows. As Example 2 shows, the raw rate can rank the wrong filter first. Normalize by loading before you decide which unit gets the inspection.

Averaging turbidity arithmetically and treating it as the combined value. Mixing is flow weighted. An arithmetic mean can be higher or lower than the true mix depending on which unit carries the flow, and it is not a reportable value in any case.

Resetting a headloss baseline without recording the reason. A projection built across a coagulant change, a valve reposition or a filter outage is not a trend, and nobody reviewing the record later can tell it apart from a valid one.

Declaring an instrument fault before verifying the process. If you call it a sensor problem and skip the grab check, bed inspection and sample line flow check, you have no evidence and the finding will not stand up.

### What to verify before you act

Confirm effective filter area against the as-built drawings, not the logsheet header. Confirm the loading basis, terminal headloss assumption, maximum run length and filter to waste practice in your approved operating procedures and design documents. Confirm monitoring locations, performance criteria, alarm setpoints and any reporting pathway in your drinking water works permit, Environmental Compliance Approval and the applicable regulation. Confirm the analyser verification and calibration records, and the bench method named in your sampling plan and approved procedure.

Confirm who may authorize the adjustment. Ontario Regulation 128/04, in sections 23 and 25 to 27, addresses designation of the overall responsible operator and operators in charge, their duties, and record keeping duties. Read the current text for your system.

For any change that alters plant flow or the number of units in service, confirm the disinfection basis against the Ontario Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water and your approved configuration, remembering that CT depends on disinfectant, temperature, pH, residual and the approved hydraulic basis such as T10. If an adverse drinking water test result arises, follow your approved notification procedure: an immediate verbal report is required, followed by written notice within 24 hours after that report.

### Fictional worked scenario: Northbrook WTP, individual filter review

Everything below is fictional. The facility, operators, instruments, records and readings do not exist and are supplied only for practice. No value here is an authorized limit or setpoint.

**Supplied values, 18:00 shift review.** Four filters. As-built drawings show F1, F2 and F4 media area of 4.0 m by 4.5 m each; F3 is out of service on backwash. The filter logsheet header for F4 has been hand-edited to read 20.0 m² with no drawing or engineering reference attached. Flows: F1 70 m³/h, F2 62 m³/h, F3 0 m³/h, F4 72 m³/h. Individual filtered turbidity: F1 0.05 NTU, F2 0.06 NTU, F4 0.19 NTU. Combined filtered water analyser reads 0.10 NTU. F4 headloss 0.42 m at 06:00 run start and 1.26 m at 18:00. F2 headloss 0.28 m at 06:00 and 0.76 m at 18:00. F4 analyser verification column reads "N/A, reading looked fine".

**Records to reject.** The hand-edited 20.0 m² area for F4 is unsupported and conflicts with the drawings, so use 18.0 m². The "N/A, reading looked fine" entry is not a verification and cannot support any conclusion about the F4 reading.

**Solution.**
F4 area = 4.0 m × 4.5 m = 18.0 m²
F4 loading = 72 m³/h ÷ 18.0 m² = 4.00 m/h
Using the rejected 20.0 m²: 72 m³/h ÷ 20.0 m² = 3.60 m/h, an 11 percent understatement.
F2 loading = 62 m³/h ÷ 18.0 m² = 3.44 m/h
F4 headloss rate = (1.26 m − 0.42 m) ÷ 12 h = 0.84 m ÷ 12 h = 0.0700 m/h
F2 headloss rate = (0.76 m − 0.28 m) ÷ 12 h = 0.48 m ÷ 12 h = 0.0400 m/h
F4 specific headloss = 0.0700 m/h ÷ 4.00 m/h = 0.0175 m per m applied
F2 specific headloss = 0.0400 m/h ÷ 3.44 m/h = 0.0116 m per m applied
Flow-weighted combined turbidity = (70 × 0.05 + 62 × 0.06 + 72 × 0.19) ÷ (70 + 62 + 72)
= (3.50 + 3.72 + 13.68) m³·NTU/h ÷ 204 m³/h = 20.90 ÷ 204 = 0.102 NTU

**Finding.** The combined reading of 0.10 NTU is consistent with the mix and conceals F4 at 0.19 NTU. F4 carries the highest loading and 51 percent more headloss per metre of water applied than F2. Action: grab check F4 by the approved bench method, verify sample line flow and optics, hold F4 loading down by rebalancing while F3 returns, and raise a work order. Retain the grab result, verification record, trend export and the corrected area reference.

checks.prompt: A declining rate filter has an effective media area of 5.0 m by 5.5 m on the as-built drawings, and its filtrate meter reads 110 m3/h. What is the hydraulic loading rate for that unit?
checks.explanation: Effective area is 5.0 m x 5.5 m = 27.5 m2, so 110 m3/h divided by 27.5 m2 gives 4.00 m3/(m2.h), which is 4.00 m/h. The 3.67 m/h answer comes from using a nominal 30 m2 box area instead of the drawing area, and 0.25 m/h is the calculation inverted.

checks.prompt: A filter logsheet header lists 30.0 m2 of area, while the as-built drawings show 27.0 m2 after launder footprint and a partition are deducted. Which value should be used to calculate that unit's loading rate?
choices: The 30.0 m2 header value for consistency with past logs
The 27.0 m2 as-built value until an engineering record changes it
The average of the two values while the discrepancy is reviewed
The nominal basin dimensions measured at the operating floor
checks.explanation: Effective area is the wetted plan area of the media taken from as-built drawings, so the drawings govern until an engineering record says otherwise. Keeping the header value for consistency simply carries a known error into every loading calculation.

checks.prompt: A design sheet expresses filter loading in L/(m2.s). A unit is calculated at 3.60 m/h. What is the equivalent value in L/(m2.s)?
checks.explanation: 3.60 m3/(m2.h) x 1000 L/m3 divided by 3600 s/h equals 1.00 L/(m2.s). The 60.0 value comes from dividing by 60 s instead of 3600 s, which converts to a per minute basis rather than a per second basis.

checks.prompt: Several filters discharge to a common filtered water header. How is the combined filtered water turbidity correctly determined from the individual unit readings?
choices: Average the individual unit readings with equal weight
Report the highest individual unit reading as combined
Use the unit with the largest flow as the combined value
Flow weight each unit reading and divide by total flow
checks.explanation: Mixing is flow weighted, so combined value equals the sum of flow times value divided by total flow. An equal weight arithmetic average ignores that a low flow unit contributes less water to the mixed stream and can give a value that no instrument ever reads.

checks.prompt: A filter run started with headloss of 0.40 m. Nine hours later the headloss reads 1.12 m with steady loading. What is the headloss rate for that run so far?
checks.explanation: Headloss rate is the change in headloss divided by elapsed time, so (1.12 m minus 0.40 m) divided by 9 h equals 0.080 m/h. The 0.124 m/h answer divides the current reading by time and ignores the headloss present at run start.

checks.prompt: A linear projection of headloss to a terminal assumption was made at hour 12 of a filter run. Which event most clearly voids the projection and requires a fresh baseline with the reason recorded?
choices: The operator in charge changed at the routine shift turnover
Coagulant dose was raised after raw water turbidity increased
The filtered water sample tap was flushed before a grab sample
A finished water discharge pressure gauge was replaced in kind
checks.explanation: Linear projection assumes stable loading, stable coagulant dose and stable raw water, so a coagulant dose change alters solids capture and voids the trend. A shift turnover is a staffing record event and does not change the hydraulics or the solids loading on the media.
