modules.lesson:
### Define the claim and the fair comparison

This is study and training material for a non-credit pilot, not operating or compliance instruction. All facilities, operators, records and readings in the examples are fictional. Numerical values are supplied case assumptions for teaching, not authorised operating values. Actual changes depend on the facility’s approvals, validated procedures and assigned authority.

A controlled trial asks whether a defined change produces a useful result without weakening treatment. Write the claim narrowly enough to test: changing the coagulant feed strategy reduces chemical use per unit of treated water under comparable source-water conditions, while the treatment performance specified in the trial plan is maintained. “The plant used less chemical” is not an adequate claim because production may simply have fallen.

Separate three questions:

- Did the intended change actually occur?
- Did treatment remain acceptable against the applicable facility requirements and trial criteria?
- Did resource use improve after accounting for production and relevant operating conditions?

Answering the last question does not answer the others. A lower dose is not automatically a better result. It may coincide with shorter filter runs, greater backwash demand, poorer particle removal or additional downstream chemical demand.

Define the comparison boundary before collecting results. Chemical consumption can mean purchased product, product fed or active ingredient fed. Water production can mean raw water processed, filtered water or net treated water delivered across a defined boundary. Energy can include only a treatment process or the entire facility. Different boundaries answer different questions.

Record the hypothesis, permitted adjustment, baseline method, measurement boundary, acceptance criteria, stopping criteria and review authority in the trial plan. Identify who can authorise the trial and who reviews the findings. Consult Ontario: O. Reg. 128/04 for the Ontario framework concerning operator designation, duties and records. A trial spreadsheet does not replace those responsibilities or the facility’s operating procedures.

### Build a comparison that can survive scrutiny

Compare periods that represent similar treatment challenges. Relevant conditions include source-water turbidity, temperature, pH, alkalinity, organic matter indicators, flow, filter availability and the stage of each filter run. Similar raw turbidity alone does not establish comparability. Water with similar turbidity can have different coagulation demand because its chemistry or particle characteristics differ.

Change one planned factor where practicable. If both coagulant dose and pH adjustment change, the result evaluates the combined strategy, not the separate effect of either adjustment. Record unavoidable changes rather than hiding them in an average.

Choose the comparison design deliberately. Repeated baseline and trial periods can reveal whether a result persists. Parallel treatment trains can provide useful comparisons only if their influent, hydraulics, equipment condition and instrumentation are sufficiently comparable. Alternating settings may be unsuitable when treatment has long carryover effects. Trial sequencing must remain within the authorised plan.

Allow for transport time and process stabilisation using the facility’s validated understanding of the treatment train. A feed change does not immediately affect every downstream instrument. Predetermine how transition data will be identified and assessed. Do not remove poor results afterwards merely because they weaken the preferred conclusion.

Use a register such as this before starting data review:

| Input or condition | Record to retain | Why it matters | Consequence of a gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chemical identity and concentration | Product certificate, batch identification and feed record | Distinguishes product mass from active mass | Active-dose comparison may be unsupported |
| Water volume and boundary | Totaliser export, meter identification and start/end times | Establishes the normalising denominator | Savings calculation may be invalid |
| Source-water condition | Time-matched analytical and process records | Tests whether treatment challenge changed | Restrict the conclusion or repeat comparison |
| Turbidity measurement chain | Instrument checks, maintenance, sample arrangement and SCADA status | Separates process changes from measurement faults | Quarantine affected data pending review |
| Filter condition | Run history, backwash events and availability | Exposes downstream costs and unequal operating states | Compare appropriate run segments or complete cycles |
| Energy boundary | Meter records and equipment included | Prevents selective accounting | Recalculate on a consistent boundary |

A missing record can make a trial inconclusive even when every displayed trend looks favourable. That is an evidence limitation, not proof that treatment failed.

### Establish trustworthy measurements

US EPA: Generating high-quality turbidity data is United States technical guidance, not Ontario law. Its measurement-chain and SCADA data-quality guidance is relevant because a displayed value depends on more than the analyser. Sample delivery, instrument condition, signal handling, time stamps and data storage all affect interpretation.

Confirm that the signal represents the intended water at the intended time. A blocked sample line, air bubbles or sample transport delay can create an apparent treatment response unrelated to the trial. Check whether stored values are instantaneous readings, averages or another statistic. An average can conceal short excursions. A flat trend may indicate stable water, but it can also indicate a held or substituted signal.

Retain instrument status alongside the measurements. Document calibration or verification checks, maintenance, sample-line work and periods marked invalid. US EPA: Field turbidity measurement provides United States technical guidance on field measurement and quality control. Local laboratory and site methods govern its use at the facility; it does not establish Ontario operating requirements.

Apply equivalent discipline to chemical and flow records. Tank deliveries, transfers and changing inventory can make delivery mass differ from consumption. Pump command percentage is not measured feed mass unless a validated relationship supports that conversion. A solution-volume calculation needs the appropriate density and concentration basis. Do not treat a mass fraction as though it were a volume fraction.

Align numerator and denominator times. Chemical fed during one reporting interval cannot fairly be divided by water produced during a different interval. Address totaliser resets, missing exports and clock differences before calculating performance.

Finally, consider measurement uncertainty. A small apparent improvement may be indistinguishable from meter uncertainty, inventory estimation error or ordinary process variation. Repeated comparable observations are stronger evidence than additional decimal places. Keep the original data, the corrected dataset and the reason for every correction so another reviewer can reproduce the result.

### Worked example: lower chemical mass without lower dose

All records and readings in this example are fictional supplied case assumptions. The baseline and trial use the same coagulant product with a supplied active mass fraction of 0.40 kg active ingredient/kg product. Matched records show baseline product consumption of 240 kg across 12,000 m³ of treated water, and trial consumption of 180 kg across 9,000 m³. Assume the consumption measurements account for inventory changes and cover the same boundary as the water volumes.

First calculate the change in total product mass:

- Product mass reduction = 240 kg − 180 kg = 60 kg.
- Relative product mass reduction = (60 kg ÷ 240 kg) × 100% = 25%.

That is a valid statement about total mass, but not yet about efficiency. Calculate product dose using the corresponding water volumes:

- Baseline product dose = 240 kg ÷ 12,000 m³ = 0.020 kg/m³.
- Baseline product dose = 0.020 kg/m³ × 1,000,000 mg/kg ÷ 1,000 L/m³ = 20 mg/L.
- Trial product dose = 180 kg ÷ 9,000 m³ = 0.020 kg/m³.
- Trial product dose = 0.020 kg/m³ × 1,000,000 mg/kg ÷ 1,000 L/m³ = 20 mg/L.
- Normalised dose reduction = [(20 mg/L − 20 mg/L) ÷ 20 mg/L] × 100% = 0%.

Check whether the reduction in throughput explains the reduced mass:

- Water-volume reduction = 12,000 m³ − 9,000 m³ = 3,000 m³.
- Relative water-volume reduction = (3,000 m³ ÷ 12,000 m³) × 100% = 25%.

For an active-ingredient comparison, apply the supplied mass fraction consistently:

- Baseline active mass = 240 kg product × 0.40 kg active/kg product = 96 kg active.
- Baseline active dose = 96 kg active ÷ 12,000 m³ = 0.008 kg active/m³.
- Baseline active dose = 0.008 kg active/m³ × 1,000,000 mg/kg ÷ 1,000 L/m³ = 8 mg active/L.
- Trial active mass = 180 kg product × 0.40 kg active/kg product = 72 kg active.
- Trial active dose = 72 kg active ÷ 9,000 m³ = 0.008 kg active/m³.
- Trial active dose = 0.008 kg active/m³ × 1,000,000 mg/kg ÷ 1,000 L/m³ = 8 mg active/L.

**Answer:** total product consumption fell by 25%, but both product dose and active dose were unchanged. The records do not demonstrate a normalised chemical saving.

This does not establish that the trial had no value. It may have maintained treatment under different conditions, but that requires separate evidence. If product concentration changed between periods, the equal product doses would no longer establish equal active doses. Retain the product certificates and batch records before making that comparison.

### Worked example: energy savings disappear at the delivery boundary

All values below are fictional supplied case assumptions. The selected energy meter covers the same treatment equipment in both periods. Baseline energy is 3,600 kWh and trial energy is 3,300 kWh. Gross treated production is 12,000 m³ and 11,000 m³ respectively. Backwash consumes 600 m³ and 880 m³ of that treated water. For this simplified example only, assume no other water losses, net storage changes or recovered backwash returns cross the selected boundary.

Start with the apparent total energy saving:

- Energy reduction = 3,600 kWh − 3,300 kWh = 300 kWh.
- Relative energy reduction = (300 kWh ÷ 3,600 kWh) × 100% = 8.33%.

Normalise to gross treated production:

- Baseline gross energy intensity = 3,600 kWh ÷ 12,000 m³ = 0.300 kWh/m³.
- Trial gross energy intensity = 3,300 kWh ÷ 11,000 m³ = 0.300 kWh/m³.

There is no improvement on that boundary. Now account for treated water consumed by backwashing:

- Baseline net delivered volume = 12,000 m³ − 600 m³ = 11,400 m³.
- Trial net delivered volume = 11,000 m³ − 880 m³ = 10,120 m³.
- Baseline net energy intensity = 3,600 kWh ÷ 11,400 m³ = 0.315789 kWh/m³.
- Trial net energy intensity = 3,300 kWh ÷ 10,120 m³ = 0.326087 kWh/m³.
- Increase in net energy intensity = 0.326087 kWh/m³ − 0.315789 kWh/m³ = 0.010298 kWh/m³.
- Relative increase = (0.010298 kWh/m³ ÷ 0.315789 kWh/m³) × 100% = approximately 3.26%.

Check the backwash share:

- Baseline backwash share = (600 m³ ÷ 12,000 m³) × 100% = 5.00%.
- Trial backwash share = (880 m³ ÷ 11,000 m³) × 100% = 8.00%.

**Answer:** total energy fell by 8.33%, energy per gross treated volume was unchanged, and energy per net delivered volume increased by approximately 3.26%. The selected delivery-boundary metric became worse.

Do not immediately attribute the additional backwash consumption to the trial. Examine filter-run histories, source-water changes, scheduled cleaning and event timing. A short interval containing several backwashes may be unrepresentative. Compare appropriately matched periods or complete cycles as specified in the plan.

If actual storage changed or washwater was recovered, the simplified subtraction would be insufficient. Use the facility’s documented water balance. If extra equipment operated outside the selected energy meter, the energy comparison would also be incomplete. Arithmetic cannot repair an incorrectly drawn boundary.

### Set stopping criteria and interpret changed conditions

Define stopping criteria before observing the result. Each criterion should identify the monitored condition, governing source, responsible role, required notification and facility-approved response. Criteria may address treatment performance, loss of reliable monitoring, equipment failure, movement outside the authorised trial envelope or inability to maintain required disinfection conditions. Do not wait for a formal limit exceedance if the authorised trial plan calls for an earlier stop.

Distinguish a treatment stop condition from an analytical exclusion. Unreliable turbidity data may make a comparison unusable, but it must also be assessed under the facility’s procedures for monitoring failure. Excluding the data from a graph does not resolve the operational issue. Likewise, stopping a trial does not erase results collected before the stop.

A change in source-water temperature, pH or organic characteristics can change the treatment challenge. Decide whether the changed condition remains inside the planned comparison range. If not, report the comparison as limited or inconclusive rather than treating normalisation as a cure. Dividing by volume corrects for throughput, not for every difference in water quality.

Downstream disinfection needs explicit attention. Ontario: Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water addresses CT concepts, T10 and disinfectant-specific treatment requirements. CT is condition specific and depends on disinfectant, temperature, pH, residual and the approved hydraulic basis for the configuration. A change in flow or treatment chemistry cannot be assumed harmless merely because filtered turbidity improves. Verify the applicable disinfection assessment rather than transferring a CT value from another condition.

At review, classify the result as supported, unsupported or inconclusive against the predefined claim. Report adverse trade-offs alongside resource metrics. Retain unfavourable observations and state the conditions over which the conclusion is defensible. A supported result still requires the facility’s authorisation process before adoption as routine practice.

### Common errors

- **Calling lower total consumption a saving in efficiency.** Production may have fallen equally or faster. Divide by the matched volume before making a normalised claim.
- **Mixing product dose and active dose.** Different formulations can deliver different active masses at the same product dose. Preserve the concentration basis and units.
- **Comparing unlike filter states.** A freshly washed filter and a filter near the end of its run are not interchangeable observations. Retain run history and compare on the planned basis.
- **Deleting inconvenient excursions.** Unplanned exclusions bias the result and may conceal an important treatment response. Apply documented validity rules and preserve the original record.
- **Treating unchanged average turbidity as sufficient acceptance.** Averages can hide excursions, while other treatment conditions may deteriorate. Review the full acceptance set and relevant time-resolved records.
- **Claiming more precision than the measurements support.** Extra spreadsheet digits do not remove meter uncertainty or poor inventory accounting. Report a defensible level of precision and explain limitations.

### What to verify before you act

Consult the facility’s current Municipal Drinking Water Licence, Drinking Water Works Permit and applicable conditions, together with the authorised trial plan and validated operating procedures. Check whether the proposed adjustment, equipment configuration and monitoring arrangements are permitted. Identify the responsible operator and supervisory authorisation through the facility’s designation records and Ontario: O. Reg. 128/04.

Verify the chemical feed calibration, product certificate, flow-meter status, turbidity quality-control records, SCADA configuration, sampling plan and matched operating logs. Review the filter backwash procedure, water-balance method and energy-meter boundary before accepting normalised resource figures.

Where the change could affect disinfection, consult the facility’s approved disinfection calculations and hydraulic basis alongside Ontario: Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water. Check the facility’s alarm-response, abnormal-operation and notification procedures rather than deriving actions from this training example.

The retained trial package should contain the authorised plan, original records, instrument checks, event log, calculation workbook, exclusions with reasons, treatment-performance review and signed decision record required by the facility. Another reviewer should be able to reconstruct the comparison, identify its limitations and understand why the proposed claim was accepted, rejected or left unresolved.

### Fictional worked scenario: reject the unsupported denominator

**The facility, operators, records and readings are fictional. All numerical values are supplied case assumptions for this training example, not authorised operating values.** This is a non-credit study exercise, not operating or compliance instruction.

At fictional Cedar Inlet Water Treatment Plant, a trial summary claims a chemical-efficiency improvement because coagulant product consumption fell from 300 kg during baseline to 240 kg during trial. The verified baseline flow-totaliser difference is 15,000 m³. The verified trial difference is 10,000 m³. Chemical consumption records account for inventory movements and match the flow-record intervals. Both periods used the same product.

A supervisor’s draft spreadsheet instead uses 12,000 m³ for trial production. Its note says “copied from production forecast”. There is no measured record supporting that denominator. The learner must reject it for the performance calculation, preserve the draft and document the correction.

The worked calculation is:

- Total product reduction = 300 kg − 240 kg = 60 kg.
- Relative total reduction = (60 kg ÷ 300 kg) × 100% = 20%.
- Baseline dose = 300 kg ÷ 15,000 m³ = 0.020 kg/m³.
- Baseline dose = 0.020 kg/m³ × 1,000,000 mg/kg ÷ 1,000 L/m³ = 20 mg/L.
- Trial dose = 240 kg ÷ 10,000 m³ = 0.024 kg/m³.
- Trial dose = 0.024 kg/m³ × 1,000,000 mg/kg ÷ 1,000 L/m³ = 24 mg/L.
- Relative dose increase = [(24 mg/L − 20 mg/L) ÷ 20 mg/L] × 100% = 20%.

**Answer:** total product consumption decreased by 20%, but product use per unit water increased by 20%. The efficiency claim is unsupported.

The fictional source-water log also records a change in raw-water condition during the trial. Therefore, the increased dose cannot be attributed solely to the changed feed strategy. Retain the totaliser exports, matched consumption records, corrected workbook and source-water log. Review treatment performance separately against the authorised trial criteria. Consistent with the measurement-chain emphasis in US EPA: Generating high-quality turbidity data, verify supporting measurement quality before interpreting trends. That source is United States technical guidance, not Ontario law.

checks.explanation: A flat trend may represent stable water or a held signal, so the measurement chain needs review. A monthly average cannot establish whether the underlying signal was valid. Sources: supplied module, 'Establish trustworthy measurements'; US EPA, 'Generating high-quality turbidity data', United States technical guidance, not Ontario law.

checks.prompt: Fictional training case, supplied assumptions: 150 kg of product was fed during production of 10,000 m³ of treated water, with matched times and boundaries. What was the product use per volume?
choices: 1.5 mg/L of product.
15 mg/L of product fed.
150 mg/L of active ingredient.
0.015 mg/L of product.
checks.explanation: 150 kg ÷ 10,000 m³ = 0.015 kg/m³ = 15 mg/L. The 0.015 mg/L option incorrectly retains the numerical value after changing units. Active dose also requires a concentration basis. These are supplied teaching assumptions, not authorised operating values. Source: supplied module, worked example.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional teaching case: liquid aluminium sulphate has a density of 1.245 g/mL and is 49.0 percent by mass as alum. You dilute 10.0 mL of neat product to a final volume of 1.000 L. What is the bench stock strength as alum?
choices: 6.10 mg/mL
4.90 mg/mL
12.45 mg/mL
61.0 mg/mL
finalAssessment.explanation: 1.245 g/mL times 1000 mL times 0.490 gives 610 g alum per litre of neat product, and 10.0 mL of that product supplies 6.10 g into 1.000 L, so 6.10 mg/mL. The 61.0 mg/mL answer comes from forgetting the 100 fold dilution of 10.0 mL into 1.000 L.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional case: a 1.50 L jar, bench stock of 5.00 mg/mL as alum, target 24.0 mg/L as alum. What stock volume is needed, and what dose is delivered after correcting for the volume added?
choices: 14.4 mL of stock, delivering about 23.8 mg/L
7.20 mL of stock, delivering about 23.9 mg/L as alum
7.20 mL of stock, delivering the full 24.0 mg/L as alum
4.80 mL of stock, delivering about 23.9 mg/L
finalAssessment.explanation: 24.0 mg/L times 1.50 L is 36.0 mg, and 36.0 mg divided by 5.00 mg/mL is 7.20 mL. Final volume becomes 1.5072 L, so the delivered dose is 36.0 mg divided by 1.5072 L, about 23.9 mg/L. Reporting the full 24.0 mg/L ignores the volume correction step.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional case: delivered dose 25.9 mg/L as alum, textbook factor 0.505 mg alkalinity as CaCO3 consumed per mg of alum, raw alkalinity 38 mg/L as CaCO3. What is the estimated remaining alkalinity?
choices: About 13.1 mg/L as CaCO3 remaining
About 32.5 mg/L as CaCO3 remaining
About 24.9 mg/L as CaCO3 remaining
About 12.1 mg/L as CaCO3 remaining
finalAssessment.explanation: 25.9 mg/L times 0.505 is about 13.1 mg/L as CaCO3 consumed, and 38 minus 13.1 leaves about 24.9 mg/L as CaCO3. The 13.1 mg/L option reports the consumption itself rather than what remains in the water.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional run with independently dosed triplicate jars per dose. Pooled repeatability standard deviation is 0.060 NTU, n = 3 per dose, and t = 2.776 at 4 degrees of freedom. The two dose means differ by 0.11 NTU settled. What does this support?
choices: The gap is above the 0.098 NTU least significant difference, so it is dose driven
The gap is meaningful because triplicate jars remove instrument noise fully
The gap proves the higher dose will also lower filtered water turbidity
The gap is below the 0.136 NTU least significant difference, within run noise
finalAssessment.explanation: Standard error of the difference is 0.060 times the square root of two thirds, about 0.049 NTU, and 2.776 times 0.049 gives a least significant difference near 0.136 NTU, which exceeds the observed 0.11 NTU. The 0.098 NTU figure omits the multiplier for two means and wrongly declares a difference.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional runs: on day 1 the gap between two doses exceeded that run's least significant difference, while on day 2, with different raw water and temperature, the same two doses differed by less than the run noise. What conclusion is defensible?
choices: Repeatability was adequate, yet a persistent dose effect is not established
Day 1 proves causation, so the higher dose can be set at the plant now
Day 2 was invalid because the earlier significant result already settled it
The two doses are equivalent, so the lower dose should be adopted permanently
finalAssessment.explanation: Replication shows the bench method could resolve differences, but a result that does not persist across raw water and temperature changes does not support a causal or transferable conclusion. Treating day 1 as proof and setting a plant dose skips both further runs and the facility approval and procedure that govern any full scale change.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional lot data supplied for this item: 49.0 percent w/w as dry alum, 8.20 percent w/w as Al2O3, density 1.32 kg/L. The pump delivers 15.0 L/h into 260 m3/h measured at the injection point. What is the dose expressed as Al2O3?
choices: 8.2 mg/L as Al2O3
6.2 mg/L as Al2O3
37.3 mg/L as Al2O3
3.3 mg/L as Al2O3
finalAssessment.explanation: 15.0 L/h x 1.32 kg/L = 19.8 kg/h product, x 0.0820 = 1.624 kg/h as Al2O3, divided by 260 m3/h = 0.006246 kg/m3, x 1000 = 6.2 mg/L. The 37.3 mg/L figure is the same feed on the dry alum product basis, which is a different basis and not what was asked.

finalAssessment.prompt: At a fictional plant the pump indicates 20.0 L/h. Three draws average 1140 mL over 4.00 min each. If the site procedure permits a setpoint correction, what indicated rate would deliver 20.0 L/h actual?
choices: 22.9 L/h indicated
20.0 L/h indicated
23.4 L/h indicated
17.1 L/h indicated
finalAssessment.explanation: 1140 mL / 4.00 min x 60 / 1000 = 17.1 L/h measured. Correction factor is 20.0 / 17.1 = 1.1696, so 20.0 x 1.1696 = 23.4 L/h indicated. The 22.9 L/h option adds the 14.5 percent deviation instead of dividing by the ratio. Any corrected setpoint must keep the dose inside the range the plant is approved and validated to run, and the root cause still needs investigation.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional check: indication 14.0 L/h, draws of 705, 698 and 702 mL each over 3.00 min, combined reading and timing uncertainty about 1.0 percent. What is the defensible conclusion?
choices: About 14.0 L/h measured, so a 1.0 percent low bias is proven
About 42.1 L/h measured, so the pump is grossly over feeding
About 0.23 L/h measured, so the pump has very nearly stalled
About 14.0 L/h measured, deviation inside noise, no bias shown
finalAssessment.explanation: Mean draw is 701.7 mL, giving 701.7 / 3.00 x 60 / 1000 = 14.03 L/h and a deviation of about +0.2 percent, which is smaller than both the 1.0 percent uncertainty and the draw spread, so no bias is demonstrated and the result is simply recorded. Calling a 0.2 percent difference a proven bias treats scatter as a real trend.

finalAssessment.prompt: Supplied case assumptions: hypochlorite labelled 120 g/L available chlorine, density 1.20 kg/L, fed at 4.0 L/h into 300 m3/h at the injection point. What is the dose as available chlorine?
choices: 1.6 mg/L as available chlorine
1.9 mg/L as available chlorine
0.5 mg/L as available chlorine
13.3 mg/L as available chlorine
finalAssessment.explanation: 4.0 L/h x 120 g/L = 480 g/h = 0.48 kg/h, divided by 300 m3/h = 0.0016 kg/m3, x 1000 = 1.6 mg/L. The 1.9 mg/L answer comes from multiplying 1.20 kg/L by 0.12, mixing weight per volume with weight per weight and overstating active chlorine by about 20 percent. Actual residual targets are set by the facility approval, not by this example.

finalAssessment.prompt: At a fictional plant, coagulant is injected at a rapid mix basin receiving 180 m3/h, while total production across two trains is 300 m3/h. The pump delivers 10.0 L/h of product at 1.30 kg/L and 48.0 percent w/w active. What dose reaches the injection point?
choices: 13.0 mg/L as active chemical
34.7 mg/L as active chemical
20.8 mg/L as active chemical
26.0 mg/L as active chemical
finalAssessment.explanation: Active mass rate is 10.0 x 1.30 x 0.480 = 6.24 kg/h, and the correct denominator is the 180 m3/h actually passing the injection point, giving 6.24 / 180 x 1000 = 34.7 mg/L. The 20.8 mg/L option uses total plant production of 300 m3/h and understates the dose that the water at that basin really receives.

finalAssessment.prompt: Filter A shows a headloss rate of 0.060 m/h at a loading rate of 4.00 m/h. Filter B shows 0.045 m/h at 2.50 m/h. Which unit develops more headloss per metre of water applied, and by about how much?
choices: Filter B, by about 50 percent
Filter A, by about 75 percent
Filter B, by about 20 percent
Filter A, by about 33 percent
finalAssessment.explanation: Specific headloss development is headloss rate divided by loading rate. Filter A gives 0.0150 and Filter B gives 0.0180 m per m applied, so B is about 20 percent higher. Ranking on the raw rate alone points at Filter A, which is only busier, not dirtier per litre filtered.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional plant holds production at 500 m3/h with five filters of 25.0 m2 each. Flows are F1 140, F2 120, F3 110, F4 80 and F5 50 m3/h. F5 goes to backwash and the split stays proportional among the other four. What is the new F1 loading rate?
finalAssessment.explanation: The four remaining units previously carried 450 m3/h, so F1 takes 500 x (140 divided by 450) = 155.6 m3/h, and 155.6 divided by 25.0 m2 is 6.22 m/h. The 5.00 m/h answer is the plant average over the area still in service and hides the step increase landing on F1.

finalAssessment.prompt: Four filters discharge to a common header. Flows are 80, 80, 40 and 100 m3/h with filtered turbidities of 0.05, 0.06, 0.30 and 0.07 NTU in that order. What is the combined filtered water turbidity?
choices: 0.09 NTU
0.12 NTU
0.15 NTU
0.30 NTU
finalAssessment.explanation: Flow weighted numerator is 4.0 + 4.8 + 12.0 + 7.0 = 27.8 m3.NTU/h, divided by 300 m3/h gives 0.093 NTU, reported as about 0.09 NTU. The 0.12 NTU choice is the equal weight arithmetic average, which is not the mixed value of the header.

finalAssessment.prompt: A filter run began at 02:00 with headloss 0.30 m. At 12:00 headloss reads 1.05 m under steady loading. The fictional plant procedure uses a terminal headloss assumption of 2.55 m and a maximum run assumption of 96 h. What is the projected total run length?
choices: About 96 h of total run
About 30 h of total run
About 20 h of total run
About 34 h of total run
finalAssessment.explanation: Rate is (1.05 minus 0.30) divided by 10 h = 0.075 m/h. Remaining headloss of 1.50 m divided by 0.075 m/h is 20 h, added to the 10 h already run gives about 30 h. The 34 h answer divides the full terminal assumption by the rate and ignores the 10 h already elapsed.

finalAssessment.prompt: Combined filtered water turbidity reads 0.10 NTU and satisfies the facility performance criterion, while individual filter F3 reads 0.32 NTU and rising. F3 carries the lowest flow of four units. What is the most defensible next step?
choices: Report the arithmetic average of the four units instead of the mix
Accept the combined value because it satisfies the plant criterion
Verify the F3 turbidimeter and flow record, then act per procedure
Increase F3 flow so its turbidity is diluted in the combined stream
finalAssessment.explanation: A per unit reading identifies which unit produced the result, so the measurement quality and the unit condition are checked first and the approved operating procedure and facility approval govern the response. Accepting the combined value lets a low flow unit hide behind dilution.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional training case, supplied assumptions: baseline fed 300 kg product at active mass fraction 0.40 across 12,000 m³; trial fed 240 kg at 0.50 across 15,000 m³. Times and boundaries match. What is the active-dose reduction?
choices: A 36% reduction in active ingredient dose.
A 25% reduction in active chemical dose.
A 0% reduction in active dose.
A 20% reduction in active dose.
finalAssessment.explanation: Baseline active dose is 300 × 0.40 ÷ 12,000 × 1,000 = 10 mg/L. Trial active dose is 240 × 0.50 ÷ 15,000 × 1,000 = 8 mg/L, a 20% reduction. The tempting 36% result compares product dose without accounting for the different active fractions. These supplied assumptions establish a calculation, not acceptable treatment or authorised values. Source: supplied module, measurement boundaries and worked example.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional training case, supplied assumptions: matched process-energy records show baseline 12,000 kWh for 10,000 m³ net treated water and trial 10,800 kWh for 8,000 m³. What happened to energy use per net treated volume?
choices: It rose by 12.5% per net treated volume.
It fell by 20% across the defined net treated-water boundary.
It fell by 10% per net treated volume.
It stayed unchanged per net treated volume.
finalAssessment.explanation: Baseline intensity is 1.20 kWh/m³ and trial intensity is 1.35 kWh/m³. The increase is (1.35 − 1.20) ÷ 1.20 × 100% = 12.5%. Total energy fell by 10%, but output fell more, so that total does not demonstrate efficiency savings. All values are supplied teaching assumptions. Source: supplied module, normalisation and energy-boundary discussion.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional training case: the authorised study plan pauses the trial if reliable filter-effluent monitoring is lost. Chemical use falls, but SCADA repeats a stored value while the analyser is faulted. Which evaluation follows the plan?
choices: End the evaluation and classify the analyser fault as treatment failure.
Pause under the plan, flag affected data and seek the designated review.
Continue the trial and use the repeated value as evidence of stable treatment.
Continue the trial while replacing fault-period values with the preceding daily average.
finalAssessment.explanation: The scenario's predefined stopping condition has been met, and the unreliable readings cannot establish maintained performance. Continuing because chemical use fell confuses resource savings with treatment evidence. An instrument fault alone also does not prove treatment failure. This is evaluation of a fictional plan, not operating instruction. Source: supplied module, trial planning and measurement-chain discussion.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional training case: a claim attributes savings solely to coagulant feed strategy. During the trial, pH adjustment also changes and results improve. Which reviewer conclusion best fits the evidence?
choices: Attribute the improvement to feed strategy because it was the stated hypothesis.
Attribute the improvement to pH adjustment because coagulation depends on chemistry.
Treat the result as evidence about the combined strategy, subject to other trial checks.
Separate the effects by assigning the entire chemical saving to feed strategy and the entire treatment improvement to pH.
finalAssessment.explanation: Changing feed strategy and pH adjustment together prevents separate attribution without further evidence. The original hypothesis does not establish causation. A later comparison intended to separate effects would need an authorised design. Source: supplied module, 'Build a comparison that can survive scrutiny'. Ontario O. Reg. 128/04 provides the relevant operator designation, duties and records framework, not automatic trial authorisation.

finalAssessment.prompt: Fictional training case: chemical feed totals and water totals cover different shifts, with clock offsets not yet resolved. Treatment records are valid and favourable. How should a reviewer classify a spreadsheet's apparent resource saving?
choices: Conservative, because clock differences generally reduce the calculated saving.
Evidence of treatment failure, requiring rejection of all otherwise valid process records.
Demonstrated, because favourable treatment records validate the normalisation.
Unsupported until numerator and denominator intervals are reconciled.
finalAssessment.explanation: Normalisation requires chemical and water quantities from aligned intervals. Valid treatment records answer a different question and cannot repair mismatched resource accounting. The gap makes the saving unsupported, not proof of treatment failure. Source: supplied module, 'Establish trustworthy measurements'.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Fictional teaching case: liquid alum has a density of 1.300 g/mL and is 47.0 percent by mass as alum. You dilute 12.0 mL of the neat product to a final volume of 1.000 L. What is the resulting bench stock strength as alum?
choices: 7.33 mg/mL
5.64 mg/mL
15.6 mg/mL
6.11 mg/mL
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: 1.300 g/mL times 1000 mL times 0.470 gives 611 g alum per litre of product, and 12.0 mL supplies 7.33 g into 1.000 L, so 7.33 mg/mL. The 6.11 mg/mL answer assumes a 10.0 mL aliquot instead of the 12.0 mL actually diluted.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Fictional case: a 2.00 L jar, bench stock of 6.00 mg/mL as alum, target 28.0 mg/L as alum. What stock volume is required, and what dose is delivered once the added volume is accounted for?
choices: 18.7 mL of stock, delivering about 27.7 mg/L
9.33 mL of stock, delivering about 27.9 mg/L as alum
9.33 mL of stock, delivering the full 28.0 mg/L as alum
4.67 mL of stock, delivering about 27.9 mg/L
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: 28.0 mg/L times 2.00 L is 56.0 mg, divided by 6.00 mg/mL gives 9.33 mL. Final volume is 2.00933 L, so the delivered dose is about 27.9 mg/L as alum. Stating the full 28.0 mg/L skips the volume correction that the bench sheet should record.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Fictional case: a jar received a delivered dose of 27.9 mg/L as alum, and the aluminium fraction for this hydrate is 0.0908 g Al per g of alum. What is the dose expressed on the aluminium basis?
choices: About 5.06 mg/L as Al
About 12.5 mg/L as Al
About 2.53 mg/L as Al
About 0.25 mg/L as Al
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: 27.9 mg/L times 0.0908 gives about 2.53 mg/L as Al, which matters because plant records and supplier sheets may use different bases. The 0.25 mg/L answer is a decimal slip of a factor of ten and would badly understate the aluminium applied.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Fictional run with independently dosed triplicate jars per dose. Pooled repeatability standard deviation is 0.040 NTU, n = 3 per dose, t = 2.776 at 4 degrees of freedom, and the dose means differ by 0.12 NTU settled. What does this support?
choices: 0.12 NTU is below the 0.111 NTU least significant difference for this run
0.12 NTU confirms the dose effect will hold across other raw water temperatures
0.12 NTU is meaningless because triplicates cannot detect gaps under 0.2 NTU
0.12 NTU exceeds the 0.091 NTU least significant difference for this run
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Standard error of the difference is 0.040 times 0.8165, about 0.0327 NTU, and 2.776 times that gives about 0.091 NTU, which the 0.12 NTU gap exceeds for this run only. Claiming the effect will hold at other temperatures moves from repeatability to a causal claim that one run cannot support.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Fictional run: a 500 mg/L stock is used for doses of 18 to 38 mg/L as alum in 2.00 L jars, requiring roughly 72 to 152 mL of stock per jar. Why is this run not interpretable as a dose comparison?
choices: Raw water is diluted in proportion to dose, so the run is confounded
Pipette error dominates because the additions are far too small
The stock will not dissolve at 500 mg/L, so dosing is inaccurate
Settling time must be extended whenever the added volume exceeds 50 mL
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Adding 72 to 152 mL to a 2.00 L jar dilutes raw turbidity and alkalinity by several percent, and the dilution grows with dose, so dose and dilution vary together. Pipette error is the opposite problem and applies when additions fall below about 1 mL.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Fictional case: a jar test optimum is reported as 3.0 mg/L as Al. Product is 8.40 percent w/w as Al2O3, density 1.34 kg/L, and flow at the injection point is 250 m3/h. Al is 0.5292 of Al2O3 by mass. What solution feed rate is needed?
choices: 3.5 L/h of product
12.6 L/h of product
6.7 L/h of product
16.9 L/h of product
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: 3.0 mg/L as Al divided by 0.5292 = 5.67 mg/L as Al2O3; x 250 m3/h = 1.417 kg/h as Al2O3; divided by 0.0840 = 16.87 kg/h product; divided by 1.34 kg/L = 12.6 L/h. The 6.7 L/h answer treats the Al figure as if it were already an Al2O3 figure, so the plant would feed far less coagulant than the jar test called for.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Fictional drawdown record: indication 9.0 L/h, draws of 420, 428 and 424 mL each over 3.00 min. What are the measured delivery and the deviation from indication?
choices: 8.48 L/h measured, about -0.5 percent deviation
14.1 L/h measured, about +57 percent deviation
8.48 L/h measured, about -5.8 percent deviation
8.48 L/h measured, about -6.1 percent deviation
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Mean draw is 424 mL, so 424 / 3.00 x 60 / 1000 = 8.48 L/h, and (8.48 minus 9.0) / 9.0 x 100 = -5.8 percent. The -6.1 percent option divides the 0.52 L/h difference by the measured rate rather than the indicated rate, which is not the deviation from indication.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Fictional plant: indication 16.0 L/h but verified delivery is 14.4 L/h. Lot data are density 1.33 kg/L and 48.5 percent w/w dry alum, with 200 m3/h at the injection point. What dose is actually being delivered?
choices: 51.6 mg/L as dry alum
95.8 mg/L as dry alum
34.9 mg/L as dry alum
46.4 mg/L as dry alum
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: 14.4 x 1.33 = 19.15 kg/h product, x 0.485 = 9.29 kg/h dry alum, divided by 200 m3/h x 1000 = 46.4 mg/L. The 51.6 mg/L answer uses the 16.0 L/h indication, which is exactly the error the drawdown check exists to catch, since indication is not a measurement of delivery.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A hypochlorite data sheet for a fictional lot lists 150 g/L available chlorine and density 1.21 kg/L, with the label stating 15 percent by volume. At a verified 5.0 L/h, what is the available chlorine mass rate?
choices: 0.75 kg/h of available chlorine
0.91 kg/h of available chlorine
0.62 kg/h of available chlorine
6.05 kg/h of available chlorine
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: 5.0 L/h x 150 g/L = 750 g/h = 0.75 kg/h, and the grams per litre figure needs no density step. The 0.91 kg/h option multiplies 5.0 L/h by 1.21 kg/L and 0.15, applying a volumetric percentage as though it were weight per weight and overstating the feed.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A drawdown series at a fictional plant shows the pump within 1 percent of indication at a 60 percent setpoint but 18 percent low at a 20 percent setpoint. What does this best support?
choices: A setpoint correction alone resolves the low end error permanently.
Delivery must be verified at each setpoint band actually used in service.
The 60 percent result can be extended across the whole pump range.
The low setpoint draw should be discarded as a timing outlier.
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: A pump can be accurate at mid range and badly off at low stroke, so linearity has to be demonstrated rather than assumed, and each band used in service needs its own verified result. Discarding the low setpoint draw assumes the outcome, and at 18 percent the deviation is far larger than normal reading and timing uncertainty.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A filter logsheet header lists 30.0 m2, but the as-built drawings give an effective media area of 4.5 m by 6.0 m. The filtrate meter reads 108 m3/h. What loading rate should be recorded for that unit?
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: The drawings give 4.5 m x 6.0 m = 27.0 m2, so 108 m3/h divided by 27.0 m2 is 4.00 m/h. The 3.60 m/h result uses the unverified 30.0 m2 header value and understates how hard the unit is actually working.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A filter began its run at headloss 0.25 m and reads 0.97 m after 16 h at a steady loading rate of 3.00 m/h. What is the specific headloss development for that run?
choices: 0.0450 m per m applied
0.0202 m per m applied
0.0180 m per m applied
0.0150 m per m applied
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Headloss rate is (0.97 minus 0.25) divided by 16 h = 0.045 m/h, and dividing by the 3.00 m/h loading gives 0.0150 m per m applied. The 0.0450 answer is the raw rate left unnormalized, which cannot be compared fairly between units at different loadings.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A filter operated at a steady loading rate of 3.75 m/h and was backwashed after a run length of 42 h. What unit filter run volume did that run achieve?
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: UFRV equals loading rate times run length, so 3.75 m/h x 42 h = 157.5, reported as about 158 m3/m2. The 360 m3/m2 answer applies the 96 h maximum run assumption rather than the run length actually achieved.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Four filters feed one header. Flows are 150, 60, 60 and 30 m3/h with filtered turbidities of 0.28, 0.06, 0.05 and 0.07 NTU in that order. What combined filtered water turbidity results from this split?
choices: 0.09 NTU
0.17 NTU
0.12 NTU
0.28 NTU
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Numerator is 42.0 + 3.6 + 3.0 + 2.1 = 50.7 m3.NTU/h over 300 m3/h, giving about 0.17 NTU. The 0.12 NTU choice is the equal weight average, which understates the mix here because the poorest performing unit is also the highest flow unit.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Taking one filter out of service changes the flow through the downstream contact chamber at a fictional plant. What is the correct approach to the disinfection calculation for the configuration now running?
choices: Rely on combined filter effluent turbidity to support the log credit
Assume CT holds because the chlorine residual setpoint was unchanged
Recalculate CT on the approved hydraulic basis for that configuration
Apply the most favourable temperature recorded during the past year
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: CT is condition specific and depends on disinfectant, temperature, pH, residual and the approved hydraulic basis, including the T10 used for that configuration, so it is recalculated against the approved basis. An unchanged residual setpoint says nothing about the altered contact time.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Fictional training case, supplied assumptions: a baseline used 400 kg product containing 0.30 kg active/kg across 12,000 m³. A trial used 300 kg containing 0.40 kg active/kg across 16,000 m³. Records are aligned. How much did active dose decrease?
choices: By 33.3% on an active ingredient dose basis.
By 43.75% on an active chemical dose basis.
By 0% on an active dose basis.
By 25% on an active dose basis.
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Both periods used 120 kg of active ingredient, but baseline dose was 10 mg/L and trial dose was 7.5 mg/L. The decrease is 25%. Unchanged active mass does not mean unchanged dose when production changes. The 43.75% option compares product dose rather than active dose. Values are supplied teaching assumptions only. Source: supplied module, measurement boundaries and worked example.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Fictional training case, supplied assumptions: a treatment-process meter recorded 15,000 kWh for 10,000 m³ net delivery before a trial, then 13,500 kWh for 7,500 m³. Intervals and boundaries match. Which normalised energy conclusion is correct?
choices: Energy intensity rose by 20% per net volume.
Energy intensity fell by 10%.
Energy intensity fell by 25% per net delivered volume.
Energy intensity remained unchanged per net delivered volume.
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Baseline energy intensity is 1.50 kWh/m³ and trial intensity is 1.80 kWh/m³, an increase of 20%. The 10% decrease describes total energy, not energy per net delivered volume. These supplied assumptions are not authorised operating values. Source: supplied module, normalisation and consistent energy boundaries.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Fictional training case: a study plan requires a pause at its filter-performance trigger. Valid records show that trigger was reached, although the daily average is favourable and chemical use is lower. Which review decision respects the plan?
choices: Continue because the daily average shows acceptable overall performance.
Apply the planned pause, retain the event and refer it for authorised review.
Remove the event as unrepresentative and assess the remaining trial records for savings.
Revise the trigger afterwards to match the favourable average.
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: A favourable average does not cancel a valid event that meets the fictional plan's stopping criterion. Removing the event or revising the trigger after seeing results biases the evaluation. Actual criteria and responses depend on facility approvals and validated procedures. Source: supplied module, trial planning, transition-data handling and measurement interpretation.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Fictional training case: parallel trains receive the same influent, but the trial train has refurbished filters and different hydraulics. Its chemical use is lower. What conclusion best addresses attribution to the tested feed strategy?
choices: The shared influent proves that feed strategy caused the lower use.
The train differences prevent any valid calculation of chemical use per volume.
The strategy's separate effect is unresolved because the trains may not be comparable.
The filter refurbishment can be ignored once both trains have valid instruments and their chemical records cover identical reporting intervals.
